#272. Kwame Brathwaite, photographer of 'Black is Beautiful' movement, dies at 85

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, announced his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

Brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in New York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

Using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

“You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model

By the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

By the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands

Throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The New Yorker.

T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is currently on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.

#271. US and UK to host Women's World Cups in 2031 and 2035

FIFA has confirmed the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica will host the 2031 Women's World Cup — the first to feature 48 teams. The UK will stage the 2035 edition, its first World Cup since 1966.

FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.

The United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, made an uncontested bid to host in 2031. It will be the first tournament to feature 48 teams — as is the case with the men. The US has hosted the event twice before, in 2003 and 1999, and is also the most successful country in its history, having won it four times.

FIFA's revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup was around $15 billion (€13.7 billion), and it's clear that US Soccer feels that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward. With the women's domestic league (NWSL) considered the strongest in the world and the US national team so dominant, securing the tournament in 2031 is a further sign of the US' committment to women's football.

"We expect and plan for the 2031 Women’s World Cup to be the largest women’s sporting event in history," Emily Cosler, US Soccer’s vice-president of strategy told The Guardian.

The 2035 tournament was also awarded to the sole bidders, England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales. This sees the World Cup return to the United Kingdom for the first time since 1966, the only time England's men's team won the competition. The women lost the 2023 final to Spain. It also means that the UK will host two major tournaments in relatively quick succession, with the men's 2028 European Championships also set to be held in England, Scotland and Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the tournament would bring "visitors, investment and jobs to every part of the country."

Given that FIFA President Gianni Infantino had revealed last year that both bids were unchallenged, this news comes as little surprise. Nevertheless, with the hosts now official, a 48-team tournament marks a remarkable advance for the women's game. The 2011 World Cup in Germany had just 16 teams.

The next World Cup will be in Brazil in 2027, running from June 24 to July 25. . Eighteen of the 32 teams have already secured qualification, including Germany.

#270. 11 Things Jensen Huang Actually Said at His First All-Hands Back at Nvidia

Jensen Huang is going to therapy for 90 minutes a day and rethinking his management style, and he says that violating Nvidia’s code of conduct isn’t necessarily a fireable offense. That’s just some of what the newly returned Nvidia CEO told staff during his first all-hands meeting on Tuesday.

Here are some of the most striking things Huang said during the meeting, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

On self-improvement: “I go to therapy every day for an hour and a half. And it’s been helping me a lot.”

On accountability: “There are rumors on the internet that apparently I’m a tech bro, and therefore I’m back. Apparently, I’m a tech bro, and because I wear a super nice jacket, that I’m above the law, and I’m above the code of conduct. That is not true. It won’t be tolerated, and it wasn’t tolerated here.”

“If one of you were to violate a code of conduct, what does that mean? If you were ever to violate a code of conduct, it is not appropriate. I just wanted you to know, it is not right, it's not appropriate, it won’t be tolerated. But ‘it won’t be tolerated’ does not mean the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door. Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments. And your management team will still make the decision. That is what is in the best interest of the company and its employees, with all the facts and circumstances.”

On his management style: “The intensity I bring elevates everybody else. But I can go too far. When I go too far, it hurts people, it belittles them, it disempowers them. And that’s not right. And so I need to go figure out how I’m going to bring the intensity, the crazy intensity, to the field.”

On women at Nvidia: “I believe we need to create and continue to sustain a safe environment for all of our women. And if I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I’ll do everything I can to fix it. We will not tolerate that.”

On succession: “All day long, this company can run autonomously, and you saw it. I promise you, whether I’m here or not, this company is wired up to execute, execute, and execute, and deliver on financial results.”

“I also didn’t believe in succession planning. Let that sink in. I don’t believe in succession planning. I think it’s flawed. The idea of succession planning is not flawed. What people think succession planning means is flawed.”

“There’s a reason why we don’t have succession planning; it’s not because we are unaware of the word. I’m the longest-running tech CEO in history.”

On politics: “There [were] also rumors that apparently I’m back because the highest levels of our government wanted me back. That is also completely untrue. Our board of directors performed their duty as they should have.”

“It is absolutely true that President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang told employees. “He gloats about Nvidia. You know he does. But there’s a question about politics. Are we now political? Are we partisan? I wanna be very clear with you. President Trump is the United States president. He is my president. And I’ll do everything I can to help this president be informed about how he could make decisions that are in the best interest of our country … We have to do it, and whoever the next president is will be my president, and I will do exactly the same.”

“Don’t think for a second that politics ever plays a role in this company, not even a little bit. We are the most apolitical company. I don’t love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”

#268. Study finds slightly higher risk of autism diagnosis in areas with more lithium in drinking water, but experts say more research is needed

A new study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC says

Cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the New York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC says the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

Lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A new study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

The researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort

As lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s important to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

Further study is required, said study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

“Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz said in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

The implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

“If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic

Dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

“It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the new research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”

Other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

Sign up here to get The Results Are In with Dr. Sanjay Gupta every Tuesday from the CNN Health team.

A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer said. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

“There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer said. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”

#267. Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans

You can learn a surprising amount from a few loose teeth.

Homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China’s Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that’s vital to the story of how our genus, Homo, took over the world.

The chemical makeup of the teeth’s enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we’d previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans.

Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. Macquarie University paleoanthropologist Kira Westaway and her colleagues analyzed proteins and chemical isotopes from the enamel of five of these teeth.

Proteins in teeth are sturdier than DNA, so they’re more likely to survive a few hundred thousand years. But like DNA, proteins contain variations that can help identify the species they came from. Four of the five teeth in the study had distinctly Homo erectus proteins in their enamel; the fifth seems to be some other hominin species, most likely a Denisovan (more on that below).

The hominin teeth and the thousands of animal bone fragments had accumulated in a cement-like rock called breccia. Based on luminescence dating (a method that measures how long it’s been since mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight) of the cave sediments, along with the ratios of uranium isotopes in the bones themselves, it looks like that breccia formed sometime between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago. That’s a wide range, but it’s enough to show that Homo erectus lived in what’s now southern China at least 60,000 years longer than we’ve previously realized.

Homo erectus emerged in Africa sometime before 2 million years ago, and they had reached East and Southeast Asia—including the islands of Indonesia—by around 1.7 million years ago. The most recent Homo erectus fossils anywhere else in mainland Asia date to somewhere between 420,000 and 400,000 years ago. Fossils from the Indonesian island of Java, however, reveal that Homo erectus held on in the islands up until at least 177,000 to 108,000 years ago. That makes it a little surprising that nobody had found traces of Homo erectus on the mainland during that 200,000- to 300,000-year gap.

These nine teeth help fill in some of that gap, showing that Homo erectus was still around on the mainland all that time after all. On its own, that would be nontrivial, but the teeth also shed light on how these long-dead hominins lived, what the world around them looked like, and how this handful of hominins was related to the rest of their species. And it turns out we’ve been drastically underestimating Homo erectus.

Credit: Kira Westaway, Macquarie University Credit: Kira Westaway, Macquarie University

Four of the five teeth that Welker and his colleagues sequenced proteins from clearly belonged to Homo erectus. Careful measurements of the other four—things like the shape and dimensions of the crown, the roots, and the place where the outer layer of enamel meets the inner layer of dentine—suggest these also belonged to Homo erectus.

But the ninth tooth, from Baxian, has proteins that don’t match any known Homo erectus variants, and the shape also looks decidedly un-Homo–erectus-like, “strongly suggesting the presence of a hominin population other than Homo erectus in Baxian Cave,” wrote Welker and his colleagues in their recent paper in the journal Nature.

But who were those other hominins? The enigmatic ninth tooth looks like it belonged to a Denisovan (or Homo longi, if you prefer). But Welker and his colleagues can’t be absolutely sure, because its proteins don’t exactly match any known Denisovan sequence, either (and there’s no clearly identified Denisovan lower second molar enamel-dentine junction to compare it to). But we do know that Denisovans lived in the wider region of mainland Asia at the time, based on fossils from other sites, and there’s no evidence of any other species running around at the same time.

“It therefore seems plausible that the Homo erectus population represented by the fossils from Naxian and Baxian Cave on the mainland existed in relatively close proximity to Denisovan hominins,” wrote Welker and his colleagues.

Now, to clarify, Naxian and Baxian Caves weren’t (as far as anyone knows) places where hominins actually lived. The bones and teeth there seem to have been carried in by porcupines, with the result that “why do porcupines collect bones?” is now part of your faithful correspondent’s search history [EDITOR’S NOTE: my search history now includes “there are porcupines in China?”]. So the presence of this tooth doesn’t mean that Homo erectus and Denisovans were roommates. But it does mean they were living in the same general area at around the same time; based on the territorial habits of modern porcupines, the teeth probably came from within an area of less than 100 square kilometers. So there’s a nonzero chance that Homo erectus and Denisovans might have interacted in some way, although we have no way to know what that interaction might have looked like.

Not long after this, our species showed up in the area, and we know for a fact that our species interacted, ahem, very closely with Denisovans in this part of the world. Exactly when Homo sapiens arrived is still a matter of some debate, but some fossils from southern China that may be Homo sapiens date as far back as 100,000 or 120,000 years ago, before the major out-of-Africa migration. So for a brief period of time, there may have been at least two and maybe three species of hominins living in the rainforests of what’s now southern China.

While the enamel proteins from four of the Baxian and Naxian teeth are clearly Homo erectus, they have a slightly different version of one particular protein—one amino acid swapped for another in the sequence that makes up the protein ameloblastin. This variant is clearly different from every other Asian Homo erectus fossil with proteins that researchers have sequenced. That means they’re probably part of a different genetic population (a group of hominins that live in the same area and mostly interbred among themselves).

There are a handful of other Homo erectus fossils from elsewhere in Asia that share one amino acid substitution with these four, but the Baxian and Naxian ones have another substitution that the other four don’t have, which means that at some point, their population branched off from the others. By plotting that kind of information on what’s called a phylogenetic tree, anthropologists can begin to map out how different groups of Homo erectus are related and how they may have moved around in time and space. And what we’re learning is pretty cool.

“The phylogenetic analysis suggests that, although based on sparse data, this hominin population [at Baxian and Naxian Caves] might have diverged before the divergence of the common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals, and Denisovans,” wrote Welker and his colleagues. That divergence happened more than 600,000 years ago. And half a millennium after that, it seems, one group of Homo erectus still living in southern Asia may have met some long-lost cousins.

Isotopes of the chemical elements carbon and oxygen in the enamel of not just the Homo erectus teeth, but teeth from several animal species like elephants (both the pygmy Stegodon and the full-size version), rhinos, apes, and relatives of modern cattle, strongly point to the area around Baxian and Naxian Caves having been a densely canopied tropical rainforest during the Middle Pleistocene.

Different types of plants use slightly different chemical processes to do photosynthesis, so they end up with different amounts of the isotopes carbon-12 and carbon-13; the ratios of those isotopes in the teeth of whatever ate the plants (in this case, pygmy elephants and Homo erectus, among others) can reveal the makeup of the local environment. At Baxian and Naxian Caves, those ratios point to a forest where the trees’ upper branches form a thick, closed canopy above the forest floor. Westaway and her colleagues say the signals look very similar to rainforests in the Amazon Basin today.

Meanwhile, the ratio of two oxygen isotopes, oxygen-18 and oxygen-16, can shed light on ancient climate conditions; higher amounts of oxygen-18, like the ones in all five teeth from Baxian and Naxian Caves, tend to signal warmer, wetter climates. All of those clues together point to tropical rainforest, a challenging environment that most anthropologists had previously assumed that only Homo sapiens were clever and adaptable enough to make a living in.

That idea, that we were the only hominins capable of making a go of it in tropical rainforests, was so entrenched that it has been considered a possible explanation for the lack of Homo erectus fossils in southern Asia after about 400,000 years ago. Around this time, the climate became warmer and wetter, allowing dense, closed-canopy tropical rainforests to spread.

“In southeast Asia, recent isotopic observations of […] expansion of rainforest in the Middle to early Late Pleistocene have been associated with the disappearance of non-Homo sapiens hominin taxa, seemingly unable to shift from mixed savanna-woodland habitats to these increasingly closed forests,” wrote Westaway and her colleagues.

Even on Java, where Homo erectus lasted until almost 100,000 years ago, those last groups seem to have lived in small patches of more open woodlands, while rainforests spread across the rest of the islands—another correlation that gives anthropologists reason to think the spread of rainforests may have had a hand in the extinction of Homo erectus.

However, the evidence from Baxian and Naxian Caves suggests Homo erectus could survive in the rainforest, “even if such habitats did not represent its primary ecological niche,” as Westaway and her colleagues put it. That doesn’t mean that every group of Homo erectus was as successful at adapting to spreading rainforests—it’s safe to assume there were cultural and social differences among the groups that might have made some more adaptable than others. But it does mean that we’ve been drastically underestimating our late cousins, and we may need to rethink what we’ve assumed were the limits of their world.

Other evidence in the enamel of the Baxian and Naxian Caves teeth underscores that point, revealing that a few of these Homo erectus individuals spent their childhoods as much as 250 kilometers away from the cave where their teeth ended up. Bedrock in different places has different ratios of the isotopes strontium-87 and strontium-86; plants take up dissolved strontium through their roots, and eventually it replaces some of the calcium in the bones (or tooth enamel) of the animals that eat the plants. So the ratio of strontium isotopes in your bones can be traced to the area of bedrock where your food was grown during the final years of your life, while the ratio in your tooth enamel is a souvenir of the bedrock where your food was grown when you were around 2 to 6 years old and forming your adult teeth. (Modern food systems are going to be a massive headache for future archaeologists.)

All four Homo erectus teeth that Westaway and her colleagues studied suggested that their erstwhile owners had either moved around between different areas or ate food gathered from different areas when they were very young. Some of those strontium ratios match bedrock as far away as northern Vietnam, about 250 kilometers away from Baxian and Naxian Caves, mostly through closed-canopy rainforest.

In other words, a handful of teeth offer enough fragments of a story to show us “that Homo erectus was not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments and that long-distance mobility into those environments may have been a common behavioral pattern rather than exceptional behavior by isolated individuals,” wrote Westaway and her colleagues. “Whether these adaptations were specific to the late-surviving populations in southern China alone remains to be seen, but further stable isotope work on other Middle Pleistocene sites is vital to address this question.”

#266. Tidal is banning fully AI-generated music. Heres how other streaming services compare.

Music streaming services add thousands of new songs every day, and a growing share of them are made entirely with AI. Some apps have started labeling those tracks or keeping them out of recommendations.

Starting Dec. 9, Tidal will begin to remove all fully AI-generated songs from its catalog and block new uploads. Robert Andersen, who leads Tidal at parent company Block, expects about 29 million tracks to come down by the start of 2027.

"We are the first DSP to do so, and we encourage our peers to follow suit. TIDAL will continue to make decisions that support real artists first," Andersen wrote in a post on X. (DSP stands for digital service provider, which is a platform that streams or sells music — like Spotify, Apple Music, or Deezer.)

Tidal started labeling tracks as "wholly" AI-generated and cutting off royalties back in July. It also moved to take down songs linked to fraud, including artist impersonation. But, according to the service, the uploads kept coming. Tidal flagged 43 percent of the tracks it received over the past 90 days as fully AI-generated, and Andersen estimates the service will turn away 80,000 to 85,000 tracks a day once the ban takes effect.

Most of those songs go unheard (thankfully). Tidal has already tagged about 27 million tracks as fully AI-generated, roughly 6.3 percent of its catalog. The company says 96 percent of those tracks went unplayed over the past three months.

Some listeners treated the ban as a reason to stick with Tidal or switch to it. "I’m genuinely so happy to have switched from Spotify to this," one commenter wrote in the subreddit, r/TIdaL. On X, another tagged Spotify and asked, "yours when?"

Other replies zeroed in on the word "wholly." One user joked that AI artists would start hiring someone "just to clap on beat." Another asked, "so 1 real cough in the intro and it’s allowed?" Behind the jokes was a practical question for Tidal: how much human input makes a recording AI-assisted?

Even some people who liked the policy wondered how Tidal would enforce it. "Fair play to Tidal, no idea how they’re going to actually catch it all though," wrote one X user. That's the challenge facing the service once it starts deciding which tracks can stay and which come down.

Apple Music is relying on labels and distributors to disclose how AI was used. Its current delivery specifications include tags for cases where AI generated a significant part of a recording, composition, music video, or artwork. A separate tag covers AI-generated artist personas that could pass for real people. In August, Apple told its music partners that the disclosures would become mandatory and that listeners would see a "Made With AI" label later in the year. (What gets labeled depends on what labels and distributors report when they submit the music.)

Deezer uses its own detection tool to label tracks that are fully AI-generated and keep them out of algorithmic recommendations and editorial playlists. In July, the company also said it would take down AI tracks used to rack up fraudulent streams or left unplayed for at least six months. Other AI tracks can still turn up in searches, but Deezer says it plans to give listeners a switch to hide them by the end of the year. The company says it receives nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks a day.

Bandcamp put a broader ban in place in January. Its policy covers music and audio made entirely or in substantial part with generative AI, and it also prohibits the use of AI to impersonate artists or their styles.

From YouTubers and TikTok stars to streamers and podcasters, Mashable talks to creators about how they built their platforms, the gear they swear by, and the trends they see coming next.

#264. Syrian refugee elected mayor of German town, years after fleeing war

A Syrian who arrived in Germany as a refugee in 2015 has won a mayoral election in the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg.

Ryyan Alshebl, who left his hometown of As Suwayda in Syria eight years ago, ran as an independent in the municipality of Ostelsheim. He won 55.41% of the votes on Sunday, beating two German candidates, Marco Strauss and Mathias Fey.

Locals cheered the 29-year-old when he welcomed his win, a victory he described as “sensational,” German local broadcaster SWR reported Monday.

“Today, Ostelsheim sent an example for broad-mindedness and cosmopolitanism for the whole of Germany,” he said, according to to German public broadcaster ZDF. “That’s not something that can be taken for granted in a conservative, rural area.”

Alshebl’s first call after his victory was to his mother in Syria, who was thrilled with the news, SWR reported.

The Association of Municipalities of Baden-Württemberg said Alshebl is the first man with Syrian roots to run for and win a mayor’s office. He will start his role in June.

'You are not a refugee.' Roma refugees fleeing war in Ukraine say they are suffering discrimination and prejudice

Ostelsheim residents have welcomed their incoming mayor. “The fairy tale has come true, and the right man has become our mayor,” Annette Keck, who lives in the village, told SWR.

Strauss, one of his opponents, congratulated Alshebl. “I wish you good luck and at the same time ask for support for Mr. Alshebl, for our shared Ostelsheim,” he said on Facebook.

The state’s Integration Minister Manne Lucha said that Alshebl’s victory showed that diversity is a natural part of Baden-Württemberg. “I would be very pleased if Ryyan Alshebl’s election encourages more people with a migration history to run for political office,” he said.

Not everyone has been so warm to the 29-year-old. ZDF reported the Syrian received hateful comments on the campaign trail.

The young politician went from house to house, promoting his election program, and “the experiences were predominantly positive,” but there was also a minority of far-right fringe voters in Ostelsheim that did not want to accept him due to his Syrian roots, Alshebl told ZDF.

Born to a schoolteacher and agricultural engineer in Syria, Alshebl described his life as carefree until the age of 20, according to his campaign website.

At the time, protests against the Syrian government that began in 2011 soon devolved into chaotic war. The fighting and later rise of ISIS forced 10.6 million people from home by late 2015 – about half of Syria’s pre-war population.

Alshebl faced the dilemma of being drafted for military service with the Syrian army or leaving the country, according to his website.

While many Syrians were displaced internally or fled to countries in the region, others like Alshebl made the dangerous journey to Europe. He was 21 years old at the time, and said he crossed from Turkey to the Greek island of Lesbos in a rubber dinghy.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel had implemented a brief open-door policy in 2015 that saw the country take in about 1.2 million asylum seekers in the following years, including Alshebl.

They were welcomed into British homes. Celebrating their first Christmas together, Ukrainians wonder if that hospitality will last

The move sparked a backlash in Germany and the sudden growth of the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the wake of summer 2015.

Once in Germany, Alshebl lived close to Ostelsheim and said at the time he felt “there is only one thing you can do: get back on your feet quickly and start investing in your own future quickly.”

For the last seven years he worked in the administration of Althengstett town hall, in a neighboring town. He drew from his experience, he said in his campaign, and made digital access to to public administration services one of priorities. Flexible childcare and climate protections are also on his agenda.

Alshebl, who is a member of the Green Party and now has German citizenship, pledged during his campaign that once elected as mayor he would move to Ostelsheim.

#262. Jensen Huang’s Return Shows Nvidia Is Too Big to Police

Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely issues to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say.

Nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs—one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. The board said input from “senior levels of the United States government” left it confident that his return poses no national security risk.

President Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. The board acted before its own investigation of Huang had concluded, and while the Justice Department is pursuing a criminal probe of Megaspeed—a Singapore company Alice Huang once ran—over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang is also under investigation, according to director of national intelligence Jay Clayton.

The experts tell WIRED they worry more about the precedent Huang’s return sets than about Huang himself. Some say the scrutiny now on him makes further compromise unlikely. But Beijing may already have gained insight into Nvidia’s chip designs and its private conversations with the White House and Congress, or, through Megaspeed, obtained the chips themselves, they say, and no one has publicly established what, if anything, it got.

Several want to know who gave the board its assurances and on what basis, and whether the government ran a counterintelligence damage assessment or simply made a political judgment. They also say the administration has repeatedly failed to enforce its own export controls, and that when intelligence concerns appear to yield to market pressure, US warnings about China start to sound negotiable, to Beijing’s benefit.

“If intelligence assessments are seen to be overridden, selectively interpreted, or publicly dismissed for political or commercial reasons, this could undermine long-term confidence in the independence of national security institutions,” says Tahlia Peterson, a cyber and technology research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a London defense think tank. “That would be damaging to US national security, and potentially advantageous to Beijing.”

Advisers briefed Trump at least twice on Alice Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence before the affair became public, and both times he played down their concerns, The New York Times reported Sunday. When the Journal asked him on Monday about Republican lawmakers who say Huang’s return endangers national security, Trump pointed to Nvidia’s rebounding stock.

“Some tech companies have become so big—and so important to the stock market—that Washington is reluctant to hold them accountable for national security lapses,” says Edward Fishman, director of the Council on Foreign Relations’ Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics.

Fishman sees a parallel in Wall Street’s slow reckoning with sanctions. “It took years of aggressive enforcement to get banks to take US sanctions compliance seriously,” he says. “We haven’t seen anything comparable in the tech sector, which helps explain why US export controls remain so weak and leaky.” Reinstating Huang on the administration's assurances before Nvidia’s own investigation has concluded “does not inspire confidence that meaningful enforcement is coming,” he says.

Emily Kilcrease, a former deputy assistant US trade representative who now directs the Energy, Economics, and Security program at the Center for a New American Security, says the administration’s record gives little reason to take those assurances at face value. “We cannot rely on the administration’s judgment, as it has repeatedly failed to enforce export controls over the past year,” she says.

On Monday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist, and the administration has recently moved to tighten rules on China’s AI industry. But Kilcrease says it acted only under pressure. “Given the poor track record on export controls and their broader accommodationist stance toward China, it’s fair to ask whether they are willing to really enforce the new controls,” she says.

The board’s assurances appear to have come mostly from the Justice Department. Attorney general Todd Blanche allegedly told Trump and vice president JD Vance on Saturday that Huang was neither a target nor a subject of any department investigation, and that the department had no evidence he had broken the law or posed a national security risk, the Journal reports. Vance then reportedly sought assurances for the board that the administration did not consider Huang a threat and that he would not face criminal charges. Trump told the Times he also consulted Clayton before pushing for Huang’s return. (“I can’t do this and then all of a sudden have somebody get indicted,” he said.)

Nvidia did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Whether Huang broke any laws is a separate question from whether Beijing gained anything through him. “Did [the assurances] reflect a counterintelligence damage assessment by the intelligence community or the FBI, or were they political in nature?” says Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations who previously directed the Foreign Malign Influence Center at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. “Lawmakers should press on that.”

Senior officials may have seen intelligence that isn’t public, so the assurances shouldn’t just be dismissed, says Sunny Cheung, a China studies fellow at the Jamestown Foundation. “However, we still don’t know who provided those assurances, what evidence they reviewed, or how they reached their conclusion, particularly when Nvidia’s own independent investigation remains unfinished,” he says.

Lawmakers appear to have seen little of that evidence. At a briefing this month by CIA director John Ratcliffe and Clayton that was scheduled to cover Iran, lawmakers pressed for answers about Huang, and the responses left some of them puzzled, according to the Times. A follow-up briefing for senior national security staff was postponed.

Cheung says the Ministry of State Security may not have needed Nvidia’s secrets to profit from the relationship. “From a counterintelligence perspective, I think people are too focused on whether Jensen handed over trade secrets,” he says. “China’s Ministry of State Security wouldn’t necessarily need Nvidia’s next-generation chip blueprints to benefit from access to him.” Insight into Huang’s direct conversations with the president, senior officials, and other top tech executives, along with his views on China and Taiwan and his role in Washington’s export-control debate, “could already be extremely valuable to Beijing,” he says.

Brandt sees the same mix of risks. “Information about Nvidia’s proprietary chip designs could help China advance its own chip design efforts,” she says. “Insight into Nvidia’s conversations with the White House and Congress could help Beijing anticipate where US export control policy is headed.” Investigators should also ask whether Alice Huang compromised Huang’s devices, what security clearance he held, and whether he still holds it, she says.

Huang successfully lobbied the Trump administration to roll back restrictions on Nvidia’s chip sales to China and negotiated a deal giving the US government a 25 percent cut of sales of certain chips approved for export there, the Times has reported. In April, minister of state security Chen Yixin made overcoming the “blockades” that limit China’s access to key technologies like AI a sixth core mission for his ministry, known as the MSS. Alice Huang’s network of chip-buying companies “lines up precisely” with that mission, Matt Pottinger, who served as deputy national security adviser during Trump’s first term, told the paper.

“A further question is whether Alice Huang was tasked by Chinese intelligence to influence Jensen Huang's views or approach to US export restrictions on China, and, if so, to what extent she succeeded,” Peterson says. The Journal also reported that the intelligence is inconclusive on whether she was actively tasked to collect information on Huang, and Cheung says “whether any such information was obtained or influence exercised remains unproven.”

Megaspeed’s purchases are better documented. A Malaysian subsidiary bought at least $4.8 billion worth of equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records the Times reviewed. Its subsidiaries have also served Chinese clients, including Alibaba. US intelligence indicates that Alice Huang was in contact with an MSS officer from spring 2025 until this fall, and that her business partner, Kang Wei, also worked with the agency, the paper reported Sunday. Her network has been linked to efforts to supply Nvidia chips to China’s state-owned military contractors. Enough has been reported to suggest that Huang, “wittingly or not, may have played a role in helping Megaspeed as it sought access to advanced Nvidia chips,” Kilcrease says.

Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Nicholas Eftimiades, a former CIA and Defense Intelligence Agency officer who teaches homeland security at Penn State Harrisburg, says Huang himself poses no security risk. Now that the relationship is public, he says, Huang has little chance of unwittingly passing along more information about US government policy or Nvidia’s board deliberations. Peterson agrees that scrutiny from Nvidia’s board, its compliance staff, federal agencies, and Congress likely limits any further exposure. But “we are still in the dark as to whether any sensitive information may already have been compromised,” she says, “or whether any resulting harm can be identified or mitigated.”

Huang’s defenders have repeatedly noted that he never received a defensive briefing, a warning the government sometimes gives Americans whom foreign intelligence services target. Nvidia’s board says its investigation will continue with Huang’s cooperation, and the company is searching for a chief compliance officer. A committee of independent directors is examining whether Huang shared corporate or national security information with Alice Huang. The board has also formed a new committee of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks.

Peterson says the company’s leadership matters. “Nvidia is an exceptionally important company, and there are legitimate arguments about the implications of losing its leadership at a critical moment in the global AI race,” she says. “But those considerations should not determine the conclusions of national security investigations.”

Trump told CNBC Monday that keeping the United States ahead of China made reinstating Huang imperative. “If we didn't do this, I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, ‘Hey, how would you like to come to China?’” he said.

For Brandt, the bigger cost may come with Washington’s next warning. “This erodes the credibility of US government warnings about China’s technological ambitions and how far it will go to achieve them,” she says. “How will those warnings land going forward, both with our own companies and with foreign governments? We risk making a hard problem harder: emboldening Beijing while weakening our own defenses.”

That cost extends to the allies Washington depends on to police its controls, adds Sarah Bauerle Danzman, an associate professor of international studies at Indiana University’s Hamilton Lugar School. The Commerce Department has few enforcement agents abroad to monitor transshipment, she says, so the system relies on partner countries to run checks and share information about problematic buyers. Singapore says it repeatedly raised concerns with US authorities in this case.

“These types of incidents make such cooperation more difficult to sustain,” Bauerle Danzman says.

Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to closed-door, transcribed interviews with three House committees on December 1 and 2. “The legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now [borne] by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens,” Senator Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican, said on X.

“I think Congress has gotten fed up,” says Kilcrease, who cites bipartisan concern about Megaspeed and what she calls the administration’s broader accommodation of China. “We can expect hearings and investigations from multiple committees, and Congress is highly motivated to pass legislation to tighten export controls, increase its oversight of administration decisions, and bolster enforcement.”

“Jensen may be back, and he should not be presumed guilty of wrongdoing,” Cheung says. “But his reinstatement should not be mistaken for a clean bill of health. Nvidia and the administration still have important questions to answer.”

#261. Weapons, war and wavering trust: Germans want to see more restraint in foreign policy

According to a study by the Körber Foundation, a growing number of Germans now oppose providing military aid to Ukraine. The majority also believes that Germany should take a neutral position between the US and China.

For decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home. The country was firmly integrated into NATO and supported EU expansion and cooperation across Europe. It also advocated for multilateral approaches to resolving conflicts around the world. All of this enjoyed broad public support. But all of this has also changed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the wars in the Middle East. Now, Germany's foreign policy has become increasingly contentious and is fueling growing public anxiety.

Long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side. This is one of the central findings of a new survey by the Hamburg-based Körber Foundation.

In the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents said they fear further military conflicts around the world. Meanwhile, 48% believe that Germany should adopt a more restrained approach to international affairs — a five percentage point increase from last year.

Since 2017, the non-profit Körber Foundation, established in the northern German city of Hamburg in 1959 by industrialist Kurt Körber, has conducted the annual surveys titled "the Berlin Pulse." For this year's study, the polling institute Forsa surveyed around 1,500 eligible voters in September.

The findings make one thing clear: The current government's approach under Chancellor Friedrich Merz — seeking to have a say in virtually every international conflict and drawing on Germany's position as the largest EU economy — is increasingly met with skepticism. Only 40% of respondents now favor greater international engagement, down from 48% in 2025.

Florian Bigge, who helped compile the study for the Körber Foundation, commented on the findings on Monday: "This is a significant decline, especially since we have been asking this question for years, with changes in the range of just two to three percentage points."

Meanwhile, 77% of respondents want Germany to focus primarily on diplomacy rather than military action.

The most dramatic shift in public opinion concerns the war in Ukraine. Germany's military support for the Eastern European country, including the delivery of billions of euros' worth of weapons, no longer has the backing of a majority of the population. In September 2026, only 46% of respondents supported continued military assistance, compared to 59% in the previous year's survey. Currently, a narrow majority of 53% want to halt weapons deliveries altogether.

As Jonathan Lehrer of "the Berlin Pulse" explains, opposition is particularly strong among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

"Eighty-eight precent of AfD supporters oppose military assistance to Ukraine," Lehrer said. "This is an interesting finding, especially considering political developments in Germany, including state elections in which the AfD gained support by campaigning against aid to Ukraine."

The AfD has recently overtaken the chancellor's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in nationwide polls.

Support for Ukraine was also the subject of a recent poll conducted by the opinion research institute Infratest Dimap. This study also found that public support for Ukraine is continuing to decline, with a majority now opposed to providing assistance (see graphic).

One finding from the Berlin Pulse study is particularly alarming for politicians and experts committed to transatlantic relations. As the US and China are increasingly seen as rivals on the global stage, 83% of respondents believe that Germany should remain neutral. Only 15% would side with the US.

This may stem from the policies of US President Donald Trump. Florian Bigge of the Körber Foundation said of the widespread preference for neutrality: "This sentiment is strong among Germans across all age groups and political parties. In eastern Germany, support for neutrality is at 92%, compared to 81% in the west. We interpret this as a desire for security but also reluctant commitment: Germans do not want to take sides in this conflict between the great powers."

The picture becomes clearer when respondents are asked about Russia. Under President Vladimir Putin, 82% of those surveyed see Russia as a military threat. However, public opinion is more divided when Germany responds firmly to such threats, including hybrid attacks. For instance, after the attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport in early May, Germany responded by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn. However, only 51% support such measures, while 46% favor a more restrained approach.

"The gap between external expectations and domestic support is the central challenge facing German foreign policy," said Sarah Pagung of the Körber Foundation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One issue that appears to cause relatively little concern among Germans is the conflict in the Middle East, despite the devastating situation in the Gaza Strip following Hamas's terrorist attack on Israel more than three years ago.

This may also have to do with changing public attitudes toward Israel. One question in the study asked: "Does Germany have a special historical and moral responsibility for Israel's security because of the Holocaust?"

The results were striking: 61% of respondents said no, while just 36% answered yes. Among those under 25, opposition to Germany's special responsibility toward the Jewish state was even higher, at 75%.

#260. NASA may get $2 billion boost as White House seeks to accelerate Artemis

“Without this funding, activities would be delayed.”

As part of ongoing wrangling over the US budget for the current fiscal year, the White House on Monday night sent a list of budget exceptions to Congress that it seeks in the near term for the federal government (PDF).

The list of so-called “funding anomalies” is dominated largely by appropriations for the Department of Defense, including the Golden Dome missile defense program championed by the Trump administration. However, among the highest non-defense exceptions is $2 billion for NASA’s Artemis program for a “higher rate of operations.”

The funding represents a significant 25 percent boost for NASA’s Artemis program, which received approximately $7.8 billion in fiscal year 2026. Technically, the White House is seeking to increase the annualized funding rate for Artemis to $9.8 billion, rather than immediately providing NASA with an additional $2 billion. It comes at a time when it is increasingly clear that China’s lunar ambitions are as expansive as NASA’s, and there is a good chance the country reaches the Moon with astronauts before NASA can get back there.

Fiscal year 2027 began on October 1 of this year, but the US Congress and White House have not agreed upon a budget. The government, including NASA, has been operating on a “continuing resolution” since that time. The existing continuing resolution remains in effect until December 11, by which time the parties need to agree to a final budget or another continuing resolution, or else the government will shut down.

Given the broad disagreement in funding priorities, it seems most likely that Congress will settle on another continuing resolution, punting a budget deal into the new year and a new Democratic-led House and Senate. The release of the White House “anomalies” document signals to Congress which priorities the Trump administration wants to see addressed in a new continuing resolution that would be agreed to in the coming weeks, which the president would have to sign.

The budget plus-up for Artemis appears to be a significant win for NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, who arrived at the space agency 11 months ago, after the White House had already put together its “President’s Budget request” for the fiscal year 2027 process. This is the first time he has had a chance to work with the Trump administration on budget priorities, and in doing so has convinced officials that NASA deserves more funding in its race back to the Moon.

As part of the description for the funding, the document indicates that NASA is seeking additional funding for Artemis without stripping away money for existing programs in other areas such as science. “Additional topline is needed to support this effort without jeopardizing other priorities outlined in the National Space Policy,” the White House document states.

The key challenge for NASA in the next two years, as part of its return to the Moon, is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to finalize development of their lunar landers—a key untested piece of the mission plan that carries astronauts down from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface, provides a temporary habitat there, and then returns the crew members to lunar orbit. The space agency has been seeking to help both companies work through supply chain and test issues.

NASA has also been working to increase its own in-house technical capabilities to help Axiom Space develop a lunar space suit and assist private companies developing a panoply of smaller landers and lunar hardware to provide power, communications, and other services as part of the agency’s Moon Base initiative. These companies all face serious supply chain issues for key hardware components.

“Language is needed to provide an additional $2 billion to meet the schedule for Artemis acceleration activities to include supply chain acceleration via in-house manufacturing and modernization of NASA’s in-house capabilities in areas such as suits, thrusters, SLS-related hardware, habitats, and safety systems for astronauts,” the White House document states. “Without this funding, activities would be delayed, missing the required operational need date.”

Notably, the document also includes the following language: “NASA needs to build and retain the ability to manufacture complex low-rate components and major assemblies.” This suggests the White House wants NASA to have the infrastructure to manufacture specialized components when commercial suppliers cannot deliver them quickly or reliably.

Importantly, the language in the White House funding request appears deliberately broad, giving Isaacman substantial flexibility to identify the most pressing bottlenecks in the Artemis program and direct resources toward addressing them quickly.

#259. These are the animals people most want to see photographed

Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.

Originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

However, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “New Big Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The New Big 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green says that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on issues impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he says.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, says Green.

“I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”

According to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “New Big 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, says Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “New Big 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, said in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

“I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she said.

“The New Big 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of issues covered by the book.

#253. No more heated seat subscriptions for cars in New York from 2027

Services with “ongoing costs” are a pretty big loophole in the new law.

Car buyers in New York may find the cost of ownership reduces a little next year. Maybe. Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill yesterday that bans car companies and dealerships from locking up car features behind a subscription, a law that goes into effect on February 27 next year.

“People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets,” the governor said.

In the old days, the only options you paid to use after you bought a car were mods or upgrades you installed after the fact. That started to change with services like General Motors’ OnStar, which introduced telematics to the vehicle—for a monthly fee.

We end users might not like having to open our wallets each month, but the capital markets sure do, and car companies love making the capital markets happy. Which is why there has been such a push toward connected vehicles. Remote start and predictive maintenance alerts are nice, but your regular payments to the car company—plus any data of yours it can sell—is the goal.

Some automakers have gone even further. Infamously, BMW and its heated seats. Like the McDonald’s coffee lawsuit, it’s a fact half-remembered; BMW North America never tried such a thing, just in countries like South Korea and the UK, and in 2023 BMW’s board said that subscriptions would only be for software-related features from then on.

New York’s press release mentions heated seats but also calls out a number of other modern tech features: “enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.”

But the way the actual law is written appears to leave a rather large loophole, at least to these eyes.

S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers or third-party service providers from adding subscription services or charging post-purchase fees for any motor vehicle feature that uses pre-installed components or hardware that do not have an ongoing cost. As vehicles become more advanced, the new law aims to establish clear rules preventing exploitative practices and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model.

A heated seat might not have “an ongoing cost,” but the maps and databases that enable “enhanced navigation” and “hands-free driving” systems definitely do, as these need to be constantly updated. A regular cadence of software updates also generates an ongoing cost to an OEM, arguably. And car companies pay for plenty of lawyers who really love to argue.

And so, while experiments like BMW’s seat heater subscription won’t be allowed in the state, the new rule might still allow for plenty of ongoing fees for services like OnStar or Mercedes’ Drive Assist Pro system we tested recently.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#249. Giving Marjorie Taylor Greene a platform isn't good for America

Editor’s Note:  Dean Obeidallah, a former attorney, is the host of SiriusXM radio’s daily program “The Dean Obeidallah Show.” Follow him @DeanObeidallah@masto.ai. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own. View more opinion on CNN.

Last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has announced plans to protest in New York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”

But on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go

In the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.)

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.)

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.)

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”

Greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”

Now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

Perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.)

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

#248. What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?

Earth's atmosphere offers protection from a nuclear blast in space, but satellites are more exposed. We explain how radiation could damage them, why the effects can linger and what protection is possible.

A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth. But it could disable satellites that provide services we depend on every day, including some that save lives.

In the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas. If GPS were also disrupted, drivers and pilots could lose navigation guidance, and financial networks could lose a source of precise time.

We have some idea of what would happen because it's already been done.

On the evening of July 8, 1962, people in Hawaii held "watch-the-bomb parties" and followed the countdown on shortwave radio. Then the night sky lit up. The United States had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometers (250 miles) above the Pacific. The test was called Starfish Prime.

An electromagnetic pulse knocked out some streetlights in Hawaii, and some Pacific radio links briefly went down. The glow faded within minutes, but some satellites failed months later.

The air was too thin for a conventional fireball to form or for a destructive shock wave to reach the ground. Charged particles made denser air below glow, creating an artificial aurora. The atmosphere also absorbed much of the initial radiation.

Satellites are especially vulnerable because they orbit above most of the atmosphere that shields people on the ground from the initial radiation.

In orbit, the initial burst of X-rays can damage spacecraft right away. But Earth's magnetic field can also trap electrons released after the blast, as it did after Starfish Prime. Satellites receive another dose each time they cross the resulting radiation belt. Over time, that exposure can damage electronics and solar panels.

That would depend on where the explosion happened and which satellites crossed the radiation belt. GPS satellites send signals that help phones, planes and ships work out where they are. They orbit about 20,200 kilometers above Earth and could keep working even if satellites closer to Earth failed.

But satellites do different jobs. A ship's emergency beacon can use GPS to work out its location, then send it to rescuers through a separate satellite network. If part of that network failed, the alert could take longer to get through.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars its parties from placing nuclear weapons in orbit. The 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty prohibits its parties from carrying out nuclear explosions in space.

The Outer Space Treaty has no dedicated system for checking what spacecraft carry. A detonation is easier to detect because US satellite sensors are designed to pick up the signals it gives off.

Shielding could help protect satellite electronics, and backups could keep some services running. During a GPS outage, pilots over the contiguous US can use ground-based navigation aids. Operators could launch replacements, but those satellites could still face lingering radiation or debris.

Radiation could leave many satellites intact but unable to steer. If two objects collided, fragments from the crash could hit other satellites, creating more debris and triggering further collisions. If enough debris built up for the chain reaction to keep going on its own, it could continue even if no new satellites were launched. This is known as Kessler syndrome.

Whether an explosion would trigger such a cascade is uncertain. If it did, the debris could endanger replacement satellites for years.

Some radioactive particles could enter the atmosphere and eventually settle on the ground. But a blast in space is too far away to sweep up the soil and water that carry fallout from a surface explosion.

As the particles disperse, their radioactivity decreases over time. The concentrated local fallout that can expose people near a ground-level blast to high doses would be unlikely.
