#183. The battery in your Fitbit Edge is replaceable, but it's not as easy as you'd think

You can get a manual from iFixit for free to guide you through the process.

After a brief period of people worrying that Google that was abandoning Fitbit devices in favor of the Pixel Watch, the company recently assuaged those fears by releasing two new devices, led by the Fitbit Edge. It's an obvious successor to the Charge series, albeit without Google Pay, or EDA scans for measuring stress.

An enhancement that might've caught your attention is the product's user-replaceable battery. The dirty secret of most fitness trackers (and smartwatches, for that matter) is that while they can last for years, if their batteries aren't replaced, their capacity will inevitably shrink until it becomes unusable. In theory, as long Google maintains app support and compatible batteries are still in warehouses, an Edge can last indefinitely.

This isn't quite like replacing the AAs in a flashlight, however, or even the coin battery you might find in an analog watch. You need specialized gear, and the process is delicate enough that there's a risk of sabotaging your Fitbit if you make a mistake.

Google's partner on this is iFixit, which provides a free PDF manual once you've signed into their website. Before you begin, however, you need to buy specialized parts and tools, including not just a fresh battery, but replacement screws for the surrounding equipment. That might seem strange, but iFixit says that these replacement parts can only be used once, a claim which may or may not say anything about the original parts as well.

Where things get risky is after you've managed to pry open the Edge's case. Its O-ring can fall out, and you'll need to reassemble that if you want your device to retain any water resistance. You'll also need a pair of tweezers, and needless to say, poking circuits could accidentally break something, as could static shock. iFixit recommends precautions like a grounding mat, and even avoiding any clothing that could build up a static charge, such as fleece.

For some owners, the major hurdle is going to be the scale of the operation. The screws and connectors involved are tiny, even by the standards of most electronics. If your hands aren't steady, this process could prove frustrating or outright impossible, speaking as someone who's hand-assembled desktop PCs.

Officially, no. If you don't want to perform the procedure yourself, Google doesn't offer a paid replacement service. The company might conceivably perform a free swap if you've got a defective battery and you're still under warranty, but you're otherwise expected to handle things yourself. If you do qualify for a battery fix, there's a chance that Google will simply send you a replacement Edge.

As time goes on, third-party options might arrive, yet Google cautions against using unofficial parts, stating that "a non-qualified battery and improper disposal may present a risk of fire, explosion, leakage, and/or other hazards." The company is, of course, covering itself legally — but there's a grain of truth in that there's no telling what the quality of a generic part may be. Lithium-ion batteries can burst into flames if they're damaged or defective. Even with Google's official parts, you should be prepared to dispose of a battery in a fireproof container.

All this helps to explain why more wearables haven't gone the replaceable route. Companies don't want to be on the hook for their customers' mistakes, and it remains to be seen how many people will actually take advantage of the option. By the time an Edge's battery wears out, you might be more inclined to buy a newer device than resuscitate last-gen hardware.

#180. You don't have to look at your Apple Watch to get the time

You can keep track of the time without missing a beat, thanks to a discreet Apple Watch setting that comes in a few versions to suit your schedule.

One of the ironies of smartwatches is that for some people, telling the time is low on the list of priorities. You can always check your iPhone if you need to, and most of us spend hours every day in front of some form of clock, whether it's a PC or an old analog ticker hanging on the wall. It's actually features like fitness tracking and quick notification checks that elevate the best Apple Watches to must-haves.

One way or another, we need to know the time, and Apple Watches come with a variety of ways to communicate it. Something you may not have heard of, though, is the ability to get it via vibration. It's something Apple calls Taptic Time, a reference to the Taptic Engine that produces haptic feedback.

Here we're going to explain how to enable Taptic Time, how it works and, perhaps most importantly, why you'd want to bother. The short answer to the last item is that for some people, a visual check just isn't an option.

To enable Taptic Time, launch the Settings app on your Apple Watch. Next, select Clock, then Taptic Time. Toggle the feature on. At that point, you'll be presented with three options: Digits, Terse or Morse Code.

That last one should probably be avoided unless you're a 19th-century telegraph operator. Terse may not be much better, though. It uses long taps to indicate that five hours have passed since midnight, short taps for additional hours, then long taps again for quarter-hour increments. It's not hard to learn, but a 15-minute margin of error could mean the difference between catching your rideshare to the airport and having to rebook your flight.

The most precise and intuitive option is Digits. This uses long taps for tens and short taps for ones and applies that to both hours and minutes. For example, 10:09 would be one long tap, a pause, then nine short taps.

When VoiceOver is on, you can also turn on Taptic Time by double-tapping the watch face while the screen is inactive. Apple notes, though, that Taptic Time won't work in any fashion if your Apple Watch is set to always speak the time. To fix that, you can go to Settings > Clock, then turn on Control With Silent Mode under Speak Time.

The honest answer is that most people shouldn't. Even if it's just every 15 minutes, having your wrist vibrate repeatedly can be annoying, much less trying to interpret a coded pattern. That's particularly true on recent Apple Watches, which have motors strong enough that alerts can be startling, even when you're expecting them.

The main beneficiaries of Taptic Time are going to be the visually impaired. In that scenario, it might initially seem strange to buy one of the best smartwatches. But with the right accessibility options enabled, you don't need to see well to benefit from some of the Apple Watch's selling points, like fitness tracking, or controlling music and some of the best smart home accessories without having your iPhone nearby.

If your eyesight is fine, you might nevertheless want haptic feedback to keep you more mindful of the time, in which case Terse mode will be the least intrusive choice. It's also conceivable that your job or hobbies might put you in situations where checking your wrist is impractical. I like to ride electric unicycles, for example — while that keeps my hands free, sometimes I need to focus on carving the pavement.

Morocco's Brahim Diaz inexplicably missed the penalty, sending the game into extra time, which is when Senegal scored the eventual winner.

Just 10 days afterwards, the CAF issued fines worth more than $1 million (€835,000) and banned players from both teams.

Two months later, and after the Senegal team had paraded the trophy to their fans, CAF declared that Senegal had "forfeited" the final by leaving the pitch. CAF then overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory and the title. The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) denounced the CAF decision and took the case to CAS.

The aftermath had rumbled on for months, with many believing it damaging for African football as a whole.

"If you look at it critically, the value of African football will definitely go down with this," Collins Okinyo, a former CAF media consultant, told DW after the result had been overturned in March.

#177. Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues

Perseverance is having trouble transmitting to Earth. Odyssey is rapidly burning through its waning fuel supply.

Two of NASA’s four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks.

The missions affected by the outages—hopefully temporary—are NASA’s Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001, and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history.

The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover’s communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate.

One of the rover’s two UHF radios was unresponsive when it powered up on October 30, triggering an automatic switch to the backup radio and placing the rover in safe mode. Ground teams at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California later discovered the backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output, NASA said in a statement last week.

“The team has stopped using both radios until they can evaluate potential causes of the issues and one or both are deemed safe to resume operating,” NASA said.

Perseverance is now transmitting signals directly to Earth in X-band, but the connection provides a “significantly lower data rate” than relaying signals through orbiters using the UHF radios. Mission managers paused the rover’s science operations “out of an abundance of caution” as they investigate the radio problem. Their initial focus is on getting the backup UHF radio running before turning their attention on recovering the primary radio, NASA said.

“The team is hopeful the rover could return to science by the end of November.”

The six-wheeled robot broke a record last month for the farthest any vehicle has driven on another planet. The Perseverance rover surpassed the 28.06-mile (45.16-kilometer) mark set by NASA’s Opportunity rover, which stopped working in 2018. Perseverance’s odometer now sits at twice the rover’s original goal for distance traveled.

The situation with the Odyssey orbiter seems more dire. One of the four reaction wheels used for pointing the spacecraft stopped spinning in early November, leaving Odyssey with two good wheels after the first one failed in 2013. The orbiter needs at least three wheels to keep it oriented correctly.

“Without the three reaction wheels, the spacecraft must rely solely on its hydrazine thrusters to remain oriented,” NASA said. The orbiter requires stable pointing to turn its solar arrays toward the Sun and its science instruments toward Mars.

Odyssey was running low on propellant before the reaction wheel malfunction, but managers were optimistic that with “extremely low” fuel usage, the orbiter would have enough to continue operating through at least the end of 2028, said Jeffrey Plaut, Odyssey’s project scientist at JPL, in a presentation earlier this year.

That assumed no failures in Odyssey’s three remaining reaction wheels. Without three healthy wheels, engineers estimate the spacecraft has enough hydrazine fuel to last one to two months, NASA said. The good news is ground teams had some initial success troubleshooting the balky reaction wheel. Further testing is necessary to determine whether the wheel is recoverable.

Odyssey is one of four orbiters NASA uses to relay data between Earth and the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers on the Martian surface. Curiosity is still driving and collecting data after 14 years on Mars. The other three relay craft are NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, which reached the red planet in 2006, the European Space Agency’s 10-year-old ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, and ESA’s 23-year-old Mars Express spacecraft.

NASA lost contact with its MAVEN orbiter last December after 11 years of operations at Mars when the spacecraft suddenly spun out of control. An investigation could not identify a specific root cause, but engineers concluded that a radiation-induced single event upset or a software issue caused MAVEN’s flight computer to reboot, according to Tiffany Morgan, director of NASA’s robotic Mars Exploration Program.

The spacecraft’s inertial measurement unit failed to provide the computer with correct information on MAVEN’s orientation, causing it to spin in response to the faulty data, Morgan said in a November 9 presentation to the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group.

NASA is preparing to send reinforcements to renew the agency’s presence at Mars. In September, NASA awarded Blue Origin a $700 million contract for the Mars Telecommunications Network (MTN), an orbiter dedicated to providing high-bandwidth connectivity between Earth and other missions operating on and around the red planet.

NASA wanted Blue Origin to complete the telecom orbiter by the end of 2028 and have it operational at Mars in 2030. But the Mars Telecommunications Network is on hold after Rocket Lab, which lost its bid to win the MTN contract, filed a protest with the Government Accountability Office. The GAO is expected to rule on the protest next month, at which time Blue Origin could start work on the NASA contract if the government rejects Rocket Lab’s petition.

Another Mars mission, SkyFall, could also launch in 2028. NASA aims to send three helicopter drones to Mars to explore the planet’s geology and weather from the air.

A perennial priority for Mars scientists is replacing the unique high-resolution mapping camera on the aging Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. Such a capability will help identify landing sites for future robotic and human missions, including a potential mission to return Perseverance’s rock specimens to Earth.

NASA is in the very early stages of developing a mission concept that could take over MRO’s imaging capability, but there’s no firm schedule or budget for such an undertaking. NASA will likely rely on MRO for landing-site reconnaissance well into the 2030s.

#176. This helpful Apple Watch feature works seamlessly with Apple CarPlay

Some drivers swear by this Apple Watch feature, and it's probably already switched on.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

If you're deep into the Apple ecosystem, the choice between Apple Maps and Google Maps isn't as clear-cut as it used to be. The first was initially a disaster, even threatening the lives of Australian drivers due to inaccuracies. Since then, however, Apple has totally overhauled the app, and these days there's often little to no practical difference — speaking as someone who recently drove cross-country to move to a new city.

I did prefer Apple Maps for that drive for one big reason: my Apple Watch. I knew that I'd be driving for hours at a time, and it was essential to exploit anything and everything to stay alert. Linked with CarPlay, the Apple Watch offers a distinct advantage in the form of haptic feedback.

Most likely this option will already be on once you've configured your watch. But you can double-check this on your iPhone and turn off the feature if it becomes more of an annoyance than a benefit.

With haptic feedback active, your Apple Watch taps your wrist whenever a turn is imminent. These vibrations coincide with CarPlay's audio and visual alerts, so it's always clear what you're supposed to do. You can even choose different vibration patterns depending on whether you need to turn left or right. This makes it virtually impossible to miss a turnoff; the feature might even be lifesaving if you're prone to nodding off on long drives.

As mentioned, these alerts should be on by default. If you want to verify that or disable them, open the Watch app on your iPhone. On the My Watch tab, select Apps, then Maps. If you like, you can toggle alerts for Driving with CarPlay, plus any other driving, walking or cycling.

Whether or not you disable CarPlay integration, you'll probably want to leave cycling alerts on. Apple Maps can be handy while riding a bike or a personal electric vehicle such as a scooter or electric unicycle, but it's sometimes difficult to check your screen and ride at the same time. Audio and haptics may be your only practical cues to make a turn.

Unfortunately, it's impossible to run CarPlay exclusively from your Apple Watch. Even the Apple Watch Ultra 4 lacks the necessary horsepower, and CarPlay would be an immense battery drain regardless. Since Apple Watches also lack USB ports, they'd be restricted to wireless CarPlay at best.

You can get driving directions directly from the watchOS version of Apple Maps. You'll get the same sort of haptics we've been talking about, plus audio and visual guidance. If you don't have your iPhone, you'll need to download offline maps or use a watch with an active cellular plan. Many carriers charge extra for smartwatch coverage, even though you're rarely going to use your watch and phone data at the same time.

While you can get Google Maps on an Apple Watch, directions won't work without your iPhone. There's no watchOS option for offline maps, and Apple Watches are largely restricted to first-party apps while on cellular. These issues may be solved someday, but neither Apple nor Google seems that eager to tackle them.

#173. Change this Roku TV setting to watch movies how they were filmed

You don't have to leave your TV's refresh rate at 60fps.

If you were to travel back in time thirty years and show someone a smart TV from today, their head would likely explode. In addition to the seemingly limitless amount of content one can find and interact with on a modern television, your Roku TV also may have the ability to let you watch movies in a far more compelling way.

Buried deep in your Roku TV's settings is a way to alter the refresh rate, and there's a very specific reason that you might want to do that. Most Roku TVs default to a refresh rate of 60fps. While that's going to be perfectly fine for some situations, it doesn't make for the most theatrical viewing experience — for the most part, movies are filmed and projected at 24fps. It's the standard, and it has defined the way movies look and feel for decades. When you go to the movie theater, you're watching a 24fps output.

Roku allows you to alter your TV's refresh rate to match that, offering something a bit closer to the original intent of those films.

There are a lot of ways to change the overall look and display of your Roku TV, but most of that discourse seems centered around colors and contrast. Those things are important, but if you really want to achieve a "movie look," then you'll want to change the refresh rate.

In your Roku TV, to match this unique look, you'll need to first go to the main menu. From here, select Settings, and then go into System. In this menu, you'll find something called Advanced System Settings, which will allow you to access Advanced Display Settings. You want to turn Auto-adjust display refresh rate on.

It's a one-click and done solution, as it will self-adjust itself to match the native refresh rate of any movie or TV show you put on. Because films have a native refresh rate of 24fps, your TV will now run them as such. The same goes for TV shows, which may be filmed at 30 or 60fps. It's a tiny adjustment, but it's one that will make your viewing experience even better.

#171. EU enlargement: Why do some EU member states use their vetoes to block the accession of certain candidate countries?

Individual EU member states use their veto powers to block candidate countries in the accession process — often for reasons of domestic politics. DW takes a look at some cases and examines what's behind them.

It's been quite a while since the European Union's last enlargement, when Croatia joined the bloc back in 2013.

If everything goes according to plan, another might soon be on the cards: Montenegro, with a population of just 620,000, could complete accession negotiations in the coming months and join the EU in early 2028.

But no sooner had EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos made this announcement in October than news emerged that Croatia might veto Montenegro's accession unless the country meets a series of Croatian demands. EU politicians and MEPs were dismayed.

This is not the first time something like this has happened: The veto rights that member states have on many EU matters have increasingly been used by individual countries in recent years as a means of leverage or obstruction, paralyzing the EU in the process.

DW takes a look at some of the most significant cases, the background to them and what are — in some instances — the serious political consequences of them.

Montenegro is the most advanced EU candidate country, with a potential accession date of 2028. It has already provisionally closed several of the EU's 33 negotiating chapters.

As of November 23, however, Croatia is blocking the closure of three chapters that have already been negotiated.

Zagreb is demanding, among other things, compensation for former prisoners held in Montenegrin camps during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s, clarification of the fate of Croatians who have been missing since that time, and more rigorous prosecution of war crimes.

There are also disputes over the precise maritime boundary between the two countries. In addition, Croatia is demanding payment of about €2.4 billion (about $2.6 billion) for assets that belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, the army of the former Yugoslavia to which both countries belonged before its breakup in the early 1990s.

Montenegro has already responded to some of Croatia's demands, including those concerning compensation for former prisoners. Others, such as the one relating to the assets of the Yugoslav People's Army, are disputed.

It is clear that Croatia's list of demands is also driven by domestic politics. No government in Zagreb can afford to appear compliant on issues relating to the Croatian War of Independence (1991–95).

Moreover, moderate conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic, who is regularly accused in Croatia of being too pro-EU, can use the dispute to portray himself as a staunch defender of national interests.

After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU in June 2022 granted Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova EU candidate status through an accelerated procedure as a gesture of solidarity.

Many EU member states have reservations about Ukraine joining the bloc quickly. Nevertheless, only Hungary, under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, adopted an obstructive stance.

Ostensibly, Hungary's obstruction was about getting Ukraine to improve the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia in western Ukraine. But Orban used the matter for domestic political purposes and as an election campaign issue, portraying Ukraine as a "mafia state."

In an effort to appeal to widespread anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Hungary, the country's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, has also adopted a tough stance on Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Magyar's government lifted several temporary blocks on the opening of new negotiating chapters after the Ukrainian parliament passed a law in early October strengthening the educational rights of national minorities.

No EU candidate country has suffered as much or as long from veto politics as North Macedonia: It was granted EU candidate status in 2005 but only began accession negotiations in July 2022.

Greece blocked the start of negotiations for 13 years because it objected to the name "Republic of Macedonia," as the country was previously known, and accused its neighbor of laying territorial claims to the region of Macedonia in northern Greece.

The dispute was settled in 2018 through a compromise that saw the country change its name to the Republic of North Macedonia the following year.

But just as the path to accession negotiations seemed clear, Bulgaria blocked the opening of talks in November 2020.

Bulgaria regards the Macedonian language as a dialect of Bulgarian and disputes the existence of a distinct Macedonian nation.

Here, too, domestic Bulgarian politics is ultimately a factor.

Former Bulgarian President and current Prime Minister Rumen Radev, for example, fueled the escalation with North Macedonia to enhance his political profile.

Although Serbia has been negotiating EU accession since 2014, little progress has been made.

In July, when the country was still led by President Aleksandar Vucic, no less than eight EU member states — including Croatia — opposed opening further negotiating chapters with Serbia.

While the main reservations relate to democratic shortcomings, deficiencies in the rule of law and corruption in Serbia, Croatia also has its own disputes with its eastern neighbor.

These concern the 1991–95 war, including missing persons, war crimes, minority rights and differing interpretations of history. Relations are also strained by nationalist rhetoric on both sides.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Whether the election victory of the Student List in Belgrade in late October , after almost two years of anti-government and anti-corruption protests, will change this situation is impossible to say.

The EU opened accession negotiations with Albania, which has been an EU candidate since 2014, in July 2022.

Albania could become the bloc's next new member after Montenegro. However, Greece has repeatedly threatened (most recently in June) to block the accession process unless the rights of its Greek minority, particularly their property rights, are adequately protected.

In light of all this, Brussels has long been debating a reform of the accession process and the EU veto system.

In early October, the European Commission proposed that decisions to open negotiations with candidate countries be made by qualified majority rather than unanimously. It also proposed that new EU members would be required to give up the right to veto decisions in certain policy areas altogether for a specified period.

The problem with these proposed reforms is that they would themselves have to be adopted unanimously. In other words, any member state could veto the reform.

#168. Figma employee sues, alleging company forced her to confront harassers

A Figma engineer is suing the design software company and its co-founder and CEO, Dylan Field, over allegations that she faced sexual harassment and retaliation while managers and HR repeatedly told her to confront the very people she accused of misconduct.

The lawsuit, filed Monday in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, alleges that Figma’s culture of “direct feedback” led managers and HR to make engineer Serry Park address harassment herself rather than investigate her complaints. Park, who joined Figma in 2022, alleges the company’s response damaged her career, compensation, and mental health. The lawsuit also alleges that Park, who is Asian, faced racial and gender discrimination, including performance criticism based on stereotypes that Asian women are meek, timid, and conflict-averse.

“Figma was my dream company for a long time,” Park told TechCrunch in an interview before the lawsuit was filed. “It was a place where I felt that I could level up in my career, working on a lot of really cool, interesting things at scale.”

Park is seeking damages, a jury trial, and a court order prohibiting Figma from requiring employees who report harassment to confront their alleged harassers. She also wants the company to adopt and enforce a process for investigating harassment complaints promptly and confidentially.

When reached for comment, a spokesperson for Figma said, “Figma does not tolerate discrimination or harassment. Figma also does not tolerate extortion. These claims have no merit, and we will present the facts in court.”

Park told TechCrunch she initially had faith in Figma’s complaint process, expecting that if she documented the alleged harassment and reported it to the right people, the company would act. But as an engineer in a male-dominated field, Park told TechCrunch, “I don’t feel that they took me seriously throughout this process.”

Park, who is still employed at Figma, joined its San Francisco office in October 2022. Within weeks, her onboarding mentor — a fellow engineer — asked her on a date and continued pursuing her after she declined, Park alleges. She initially feared reporting him, worrying that her manager would “dismiss her reports or view her as the problem,” according to the lawsuit.

Park says she tried to avoid her onboarding mentor. In early 2023, for example, she delayed choosing a work project until he had picked one. When her manager criticized her for not being a “team player,” Park explained that she was trying to avoid the colleague she accused of harassment, according to the suit.

Her manager allegedly dismissed her concerns, saying he had “met his wife at work too” and treating the behavior as “harmless flirtation.” When Park asked to be kept off projects with the onboarding mentor, HR allegedly instructed her to confront him directly about his behavior.

The lawsuit ties that response to Figma’s culture of direct feedback, which Park alleges Field established and enforced. It says the company’s People organization trains managers to direct employees, including those reporting harassment, to give feedback directly to the person involved.

In March 2023, her manager assigned him to a major project she was leading, despite her request to be separated from him. Park told her manager that she would “figure it out,” but alleges that having to work with him affected her performance. Her manager gave her a 2 out of 5 on her performance review, criticizing her for not speaking up enough or engaging with others and for lacking presence. Park was put on a coaching plan, which she completed in late 2023.

Changing managers didn’t help, according to the lawsuit. Her second manager also refused to separate them, allegedly telling Park that someone at her level should be able to resolve conflicts with teammates and that separating them would be “avoiding the problem.” Like her previous manager, he allegedly pointed out that he had met his partner at work.

Park alleges the harassment continued throughout 2023.

In April 2024, she transferred to another team, a move she claims set back her career by resetting her performance and promotion timeline.

On her new team, which had more women, Park said she felt better and no longer had to work with her alleged harasser. Her performance reviews improved, but in late 2025, she alleges another incident of sexual harassment, this time by her new manager.

The incident followed a night out for drinks with her wife and two teammates, including her manager. The next day, during a team lunch, the manager allegedly said Park’s sex life had been discussed the previous evening. Park, who said no such conversation had occurred in her or her wife’s presence, felt “horrified and humiliated” by comments she believed fetishized queer relationships.

A colleague reported the comments to HR as sexual harassment, according to the suit. Weeks later, Park’s manager apologized in a Slack message, saying she didn’t recall what she had said. When Park sought HR’s guidance, she was again told to address the matter directly with her manager.

During their conversation, the manager allegedly became defensive, and the encounter left Park feeling “crushed, anxious, and vulnerable.” The manager also allegedly said she would never make such a comment because she had “a lot of gay friends.”

The manager told HR that they had agreed it was a misunderstanding. HR closed its investigation without interviewing witnesses, according to the suit, even though Park disputed her manager’s account.

“Requiring an employee to confront her harasser as the price of complaining — and then closing her complaint — would dissuade a reasonable employee from complaining at all,” the suit said.

Park alleges her manager retaliated by publicly berating her, sometimes so aggressively that colleagues intervened or checked on her afterward, according to the lawsuit. The suit also alleges that other teammates left the team over concerns about the manager’s behavior.

Park again complained to HR about “escalating retaliation” and expressed concern the manager would “derail her career.” HR allegedly defended the manager’s conduct, saying the manager was “within her reasonable authority” and again instructed Park to address her concerns directly with the manager.

In early 2026, Park received another low performance review and a reduced bonus. The lawsuit alleges that similarly situated men continued to receive promotions, raises, and bonuses. When Park reported the negative performance review to HR in March, she was allegedly told her sexual harassment complaint against her manager could not be “substantiated.”

Park took medical leave in March to receive treatment for PTSD symptoms and generalized anxiety. Cleared to return to work in June, she was prescribed workplace accommodations, including a graduated work schedule and mandatory remote workdays.

Park told TechCrunch that Figma approved the accommodations but had not implemented them at the time she returned to work. In July, Park and her lawyers notified Figma of their intent to pursue legal action.

“It’s really scary for me,” she said about taking legal action. “I don’t know what’s going to happen next with this, I don’t know what the outcome is going to be, but at least it feels like this is my chance to do the right thing.”

This piece was updated to clarify when Park said Figma implemented the recommendations from her medical professionals.

#165. Huang reportedly admitted to more than two affairs to Nvidia’s board

In a complete U-turn, Nvidia’s board on Monday reinstated Jensen Huang as the CEO and president of the chipmaker, just a fortnight after he resigned.

During a meeting before his reinstatement, however, Huang admitted to more affairs beyond the two that have been reported in the news, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Early in November, Huang admitted to an extramarital affair in a letter to employees. At the time, he was ostensibly talking about his relationship with Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (not related to Jensen). Later, it was reported that he’d also had a relationship with Nvidia’s VP of health, Kimberly Powell.

Afterwards, Reuters reported that he also had an affair with another employee.

It’s not clear which affairs Huang admitted to during this recent conversation with Nvidia’s board of directors.

Huang’s return was spurred by a personal intervention from the U.S. government, Nvidia’s board said in a statement on Monday, and President Donald Trump apparently called the board to bat for Huang’s reinstatement.

The Wall Street Journal reports that over the weekend, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told Trump and Vice President JD Vance that the Justice Department wasn’t investigating Huang and there was no evidence that he was a national security risk, after which both contacted the company’s board.

Huang received a “hero’s welcome” at Nvidia’s HQ, with several employees applauding his return.

#163. The clock is running out for America’s most contentious spying law

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Warrantless wiretapping proponents are rushing to beat the looming blue wave.

Warrantless wiretapping proponents are rushing to beat the looming blue wave.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Weeks before the end of the legislative session, some members of Congress are scrambling to reauthorize a controversial warrantless wiretapping authority, possibly by attaching it to a must-pass military spending bill. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD) told Politicothat Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) could be attached to the National Defense Authorization Act. It’s the latest in a grueling fight over a major spying rule that hasn’t technically lapsed.

“We don’t have two weeks to work just on FISA,” said Rounds, a member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. “But if it’s amended onto the NDAA then you can move it forward and get that done in time.”

FISA allows for the warrantless surveillance of certain foreigners’ communications, ostensibly on national security grounds. In part because of FISA’s broad scope, Congress revisits it every few years, both to reauthorize the authority and to reform it. The last effort to do both failed. Despite pressure from President Donald Trump, Congress failed to reauthorize FISA over the summer, in part because leadership wouldn’t allow any amendments — particularly attempts to limit its sweeping scope — to be debated or introduced. (Trump didn’t help matters when he made Bill Pulte the acting director of national intelligence. Pulte, who reportedly bragged about purging one-third of the DNI staff, is now the director of federal housing.) But the surveillance authority didn’t actually lapse because the FISA court rectified surveillance under Section 702 back in March, meaning the surveillance state can keep chugging along as is for another four months.

So why the urgency? If you haven’t heard, there’s about to be a new Congress in town — one that is even less likely to give Trump seemingly unlimited spying powers without some semblance of reform.

“It was remarkable watching two dozen House Republicans stand up to the establishment, stand up to Mike Johnson, and fight to reform FISA,” said Michael Baick, an organizer with the OpenAI boycott campaign QuitGPT, which has been advocating for FISA reform to stop AI surveillance. “This has always been a bipartisan issue where Americans of all stripes can agree, and trying to make deals with the establishment to maintain the status quo, while the ground is shifting, is just short-sighted and missing what this moment really is.”

“I think it’s a Hail Mary by surveillance hawks to try to ram through what they wanted to do the entire time.”

Johnson and Himes were adamantly opposed to any reining in of Section 702, stressing the need for a so-called “clean reauthorization.” Both claimed there had already been reforms. “It ain’t the same FISA,” Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) declared in April.

But the changes reformers most wanted were missing. Among them were a warrant requirement and an end to what critics say are major loopholes. Under Section 702, intelligence agencies can pull the communications of non-US persons not in the United States — that is, foreign nationals outside the country. But federal agencies like the FBI and NSA can buy Americans’ data from private brokers, a practice FBI director Kash Patel admits is ongoing. And intelligence agencies can use Section 702 to obtain the communications of non-US persons who are communicating with Americans — a workaround known as the “backdoor search loophole.”

“I think it’s a Hail Mary by surveillance hawks to try to ram through what they wanted to do the entire time,” Don Bell, senior policy counsel at the Constitution Project of the Project on Government Oversight, told The Verge. “This is something everyone knew was coming down the pike. There have been months to do this, and I don’t think anyone is saying don’t reauthorize at all. The argument is this is an incredibly powerful surveillance tool, and there needs to be guardrails in place to protect people’s constitutional rights.”

Himes, arguably the Democratic Party’s biggest champion of FISA, seems willing to give Trump one more win before the blue wave crashes down in Washington. “I made it clear to some very senior administration officials that they should get this thing done in the lame-duck,” he told The Hill, “because it’s, you know, going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the first quarter of next year.”

But Himes didn’t have the votes this summer, and it’s even less likely that he’ll have the votes for a clean reauthorization now.

#162. Pope Francis diaries recount spiritual crisis, him seeing the 'Devil'

Extracts of the late Pope Francis' diaries have been published, the first release of its kind since the 1960s. They discuss his struggles with his role in the Vatican and visions of the devil and the gates of hell.

The late Pope Francis suffered a spiritual crisis during his papacy when he struggled with how to lead the Catholic Church and believed he saw and heard the devil on several occasions, according to an annotated collection of his private diaries published on Tuesday.

Francis was pope for 12 years until his death last April.

Cardinal Victor Fernandez, a compatriot and close collaborator of Francis', collated the diary entries and provides accompanying commentary, in the first set of papal diaries to be published posthumously since those of John XXIII, who died in 1963.

The diary entries speak of the Argentine-born pontiff not wanting to be someone "who uses others like puppets," according to the accompanying commentary.

"It was all mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation," a December 2022 entry from Francis said.

Although the book does not make clear exactly who Francis worried he was using like puppets or the nature of the internal pressures, Francis encountered stern resistance from more conservative forces within the Church as he urged the staid institution to modernize.

Cardinal Fernandez wrote that Francis "ultimately recognized it was the worst trial that had toremented him ... and that he felt that he was in a continual battle not to fall into this demonic seduction."

The 160-page selection of excerpts — starting in 1992 when he was still known as Jorge Mario Bergoglio and running until a few months before his death — are arranged by theme and pay closer attention to Francis' internal spiritual experiences than Vatican politics.

But one of the three occasions listed where the late pope believed he had seen the Devil was during a meeting with Vatican officials in January 2021 early in what he termed a spiritual crisis. In that instance he even believed to have heard the figure speak.

"I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice," Francis wrote in an entry. "The Lord granted me an opportunity to leave that meeting, and thus he freed me."

Other entries detail how Francis believed that God spoke to him in his dreams, and one from 2018 stated: "Last night I saw the entrance to Hell. I peeked in to look a little, and it terrified me."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The papers show Francis to be self-critical at times, chastizing himself for "feelings of disdain, envy, pride" or for ignoring a drunken man who approached him "because I wanted to have a serene walk."

At one point in a 2022 entry he refers to himself as the "proud, self-sufficient, cynical, self-deceptive Jorge."

They also show how in later years he felt anxious to make the most of his remaining years, and regretful about some of his deicsions earlier in his life.

"I want to do good during the little time I have left, desiring to be good," he wrote in 1996 on turning 60. "How much time I've used badly! How much badly done!"

The accounts also list his regret after a visit to Chile in 2018 when he faced stern criticism for initially dismissing allegations of sexual abuse and cover-up against a bishop there before later apologizing.

"It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious," a "devastated" pontiff wrote three years later.

Fernandez also recounts comments from Francis on some senior officials in the Vatican including his successor, US Cardinal Robert Prevost, now Pope Leo XIV. According to Fernandez, Francis called him "a great pastor, a generous missionary, and an irreproachable man."

#160. Erdogan's political fate may be determined by Turkey's Kurds

Editor’s Note:  A version of this story first appeared in CNN’s Meanwhile in the Middle East newsletter, a three-times-a-week look inside the region’s biggest stories. Sign up here.

Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month announced that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.

“We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” said the HDP in a statement on March 23. “To fulfill our historical responsibility against the one-man rule, we will not field a presidential candidate in (the) May 14 elections.”

It is a twist of irony for the Turkish strongman, who spent the better half of the past decade cracking down on the party after it began chipping away at his voter base. Its former leader Selahattin Demirtas has been in prison for nearly seven years and the party faces possible closure by a court for suspected collusion with the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and affiliated groups. But its influence may nonetheless determine the course of Turkey’s politics.

The HDP’s decision not to field a candidate came just three days after head of the Republican People’s Party (CHP) Kemal Kilicdaroglu, Erdogan’s main rival, visited the party’s co-chairs. He told reporters that the solution to Turkey’s problems, “including the Kurdish problem” lies in parliament,” according to Turkish media.

Kilicdaroglu, who represents the six-party Nation Alliance opposition bloc, is the strongest contender to run against Erdogan in years. And while the HDP hasn’t yet announced whether it will put its weight behind him, analysts say it is the kingmaker in the elections.

Erdogan's 'polar opposite' wants to replace him as president of Turkey

“It was a carefully crafted political discourse,” Hisyar Ozsoy, deputy co-chair of the HDP and a member of parliament from the predominantly Kurdish province of Diyarbakir, told CNN. “We are not going to have our own candidate, and we will leave it to the international community to interpret it the way they wish.”

Experts say the crackdown on the HDP is rooted in the threat it poses to Erdogan politically, as well as its position as one of the main parties representing Turkey’s Kurds, an ethnic minority from which a separatist militant movement has emerged.

The party and the Kurdish people have had a complicated relationship with Erdogan. The leader courted the Kurds in earlier years by granting them more rights and reversing restrictions on the use of their language. Relations with the HDP were also cordial once, as Erdogan worked with the party on a brief peace process with the PKK.

But ties between Erdogan and the HDP later turned sour, and the HDP fell under a sweeping crackdown aimed at the PKK and their affiliates.

Kurds are the biggest minority in Turkey, making up between 15% and 20% of the population, according to Minority Rights Group International.

It is unclear if the HDP will endorse Kilicdaroglu, but analysts say that the deliberate distance may be beneficial for the opposition candidate.

The accusations against the HDP place it in a precarious position during the elections. It currently faces a case in Turkey’s Constitutional Court over suspected ties to the PKK, which is designated as a terrorist group by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. Knowing it may be banned at any moment, its candidates are running under the Green Left Party in parliament.

If the opposition is seen as allying with the HDP, Erdogan’s AK Party may use its influence in the media to discredit it as being pro-PKK, said Murat Somer, a political science professor at Koc University in Istanbul and author of Return to Point Zero, a book on the Turkish-Kurdish question in Turkey.

The HDP’s threat to Erdogan’s hold on power became apparent after the June 2015 election, the first general election it participated in. It won 13% of the seats, denying the ruling AK Party its majority for the first time since 2002. Erdogan, however, called a snap election five months later, which led to a drop in the HDP’s support to 10.7%, as well as the restoration of the AK Party’s overall majority.

“They are a kingmaker in these elections because the HDP gets about half of the votes of the Kurdish population in Turkey,” said Somer, adding that the other, more conservative Kurdish voters have traditionally voted for Erdogan’s AK Party. And last month, the Free Cause Party (HUDA-PAR), a tiny Kurdish-Islamist party announced support for Erdogan in the elections. The party has never won seats in parliament.

Erdogan's political fate may rest on his response to the earthquake

The HDP knows that its position is key to the outcome of next month’s vote, but that it’s also in a delicate situation.

“We want to play the game wisely, and we need to be very careful,” said Ozsoy, adding that the party wants to avoid a “contaminated political climate” where the elections are polarized “between a very ugly ultra-nationalist discourse against Kilicdaroglu and others.”

The party was founded in 2012 with a number of aims, said Ozsoy, one of which was “peaceful and democratic resolution of the Kurdish conflict.”

Somer said that the party was seen to be “an initiative” of the PKK, which later led to a heavy government crackdown on it in the name of counterterrorism.

Its former leader Demirtas remains an influential figure.

The Turkish government has been trying to link the HDP to the PKK but has so far failed to prove “a real connection,” said Asli Aydintasbas, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington, DC.

A post-Erdogan Turkey may give some breathing space to the Kurds and Kurdish-dominated parties in Turkey, Aydintasbas told CNN, noting that many Kurdish voters have recently left Erdogan’s camp. “For HDP, this is more than just an ideological choice,” she said. “It’s a matter of survival.”

Ozsoy says his party understands what’s at stake, not only for Turkey’s Kurds but for all its minorities.

“We are aware of our responsibility here. We are aware of our role. We know we are in a kingmaker position,” the HDP lawmaker said.

#159. Amazon’s Decart acquisition is a bet on using software to narrow the silicon gap with Nvidia

Jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the road: Amazon’s decision to acquire Decart‘s tech and its team for a reported $7.5 billion.

The broader industry seems to agree that Decart’s tech for optimizing AI models to run on non-Nvidia chips is worth several billion dollars. Anthropic reportedly tried to acquire the startup in the same ballpark, and Nvidia, which invested in the startup’s $300 million funding round at a $4 billion valuation, was also rumored as a prospective buyer.

Amazon was ultimately the one to pull the trigger and bring on board Decart’s co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf, and Moshe Shalev and their team, but the company is not interested in the world models they had been working on. At the heart of the deal is the startup’s tech that helps AI models run better on all kinds of chips.

By incorporating the startup’s Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), Amazon is now hoping to extract more performance out of its Trainium chips, as the company tries to turn AWS into a $1 trillion revenue business.

In its announcement, Amazon said it has worked with Decart since 2025 to optimize the Trainium chips. This deal is ostensibly aimed at accelerating that work, which could eventually result in the company offering its Trainium-based data centers, which Anthropic already uses, to more customers. Amazon has already been working to make Trainium easier to switch to.

One way Nvidia managed to leapfrog its competitors was by spending $6.9 billion to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox, which eventually grew to become a core piece of its international manufacturing strategy. Amazon could well be following a similar path.

Annapurna Labs makes for a more interesting parallel than Mellanox, however, as the latter formed the basis of Amazon’s custom chip-designing unit following its 2015 acquisition. Add Intel into the mix, and this becomes a broader story. “Most of the hardware powering the AI wave was built in Israel. Annapurna; Mellanox; Habana Labs; etc…,” VC Eric Reiner observed on X a few months ago.

In an email to TechCrunch, Eze Vidra, co-founder and managing partner at Remagine Ventures, said the deal is “a strong signal for the Israeli deep-tech ecosystem, showing that specialized local talent continues to attract major global players.”

Amazon still has a ways to go before it can make a dent in Nvidia’s near-monopoly on AI chips, but the deal could help the e-commerce giant speed up its efforts. Dean Meyer, a partner at Sequoia who co-led the firm’s seed investment into Decart, said on X that the deal “will be looked back on as one of the most strategically important acquisitions in many, many years.”

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to staff during his first all-hands since returning to the company, while attempting to distance himself from the narrative that the White House and tech leaders helped him get his job back, according to reports from Bloomberg, The New York Times, and The Handbasket’s Marisa Kabas.

During the meeting, Huang reportedly called claims that President Donald Trump was directly involved in his reinstatement — an idea publicly promoted by Trump himself — “completely untrue.” He added, “Don’t think for a second politics played a role in the company. We are the most apolitical company,” according to Kabas.

Along with attempting to dismiss Trump’s involvement, Huang reportedly said he also didn’t return because he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law” or “above the code of conduct.” He added that, “no story has been more tortured than this one in human history,” Kabas reports. Instead, Huang said the Nvidia board “evaluated the entire situation,” while receiving assurance from the government that he posed no national security threat, according to the NYT.

Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on November 12th, following reports of affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two employees, including vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell. On Monday, Nvidia announced that it had reinstated Huang as CEO, president, and member of the board — a decision the White House said Trump was “totally involved in.” Trump also confirmed that he worked with Vice President JD Vance and other officials to bring Huang back. A swath of tech leaders, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and former White House AI czar David Sacks, were also in favor of Huang’s return.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said that the government “has no reason to believe” Huang’s return poses a risk to national security, adding that the US attorney general “does not possess evidence” that he engaged in “unlawful conduct.” Nvidia is still facing an investigation over its accounting practices, according to Reuters. The company is also carrying out its own internal investigation surrounding reports that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Huang is set to testify before Congress on December 1st to answer questions about national security concerns, and Democrats are already planning to press Huang about his return, as well as Trump’s involvement.

Even after all this, Huang reportedly said he “doesn’t believe in succession planning.” He also acknowledged that he violated Nvidia’s code of conduct, adding that he is attending therapy daily, Bloomberg reports. “I made some terrible mistakes,” Huang said, according to the NYT. “I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids and of course, I hurt all of you.”

#156. Pinterest will now let parents limit the AI-generated content their teens see

Pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: Parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether or not videos auto-play.

The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.

Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta announced a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.

WhatsApp currently allows parents to adjust the level of access teens have to Meta AI, in terms of using AI to create content or having the AI respond to their teen’s questions.

But when it comes to AI-generated content filling users’ feeds and recommendations, there are few controls available on social media platforms in general, much less those provided as part of the parental controls.

This problem, parents say, is harming children’s well-being in favor of profits. For instance, in April, the children’s advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, signed by over 200 organizations and experts, calling on YouTube to remove AI-generated content from YouTube Kids and bar AI-generated videos from being recommended to users under 18.

Pinterest has fought its own battle against AI content, which still finds its way into users’ feeds even when the settings that restrict AI-modified content, which the company introduced in 2025, are enabled.

Putting a similar set of tools into parents’ hands is at least a good first step in allowing the users themselves to dictate the type of experience they want to have on the app.

The new feature arrived alongside other parental controls, including one to stop auto-playing videos and another that lets parents adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The Parental Controls Page was also redesigned to make it easier to find and configure certain controls and to allow parents to configure settings related to personalized ads.

#155. Israeli military veterans, a backbone of protest movement, vow to keep demonstrating

In a sea of Israeli flags, Yiftach Golov holds one that looks a little different.

Among the hundreds of thousands of protesters who took to the streets for the 13th week in a row on Saturday, Golov hoists a brown flag that represents a group called “Brother and Sisters in Arms.”

They are veterans – many, like Golov, from elite forces – who now feel they are fighting on a new battlefield: To save Israeli democracy.

“We believe this is our responsibility to go once again called to the flag of the nation to stop this madness to defend Israel,” Golov said, as he weaved his way through the protesters on Tel Aviv’s Kaplan street, between the high-rises that house many of Israel’s high tech companies.

During the second intifada, in the early 2000s, Golov served in a special forces reconnaissance unit. He was never before particularly political, focusing more on getting his PhD in biophysics from Tel Aviv University.

But when the protest movement against the Israeli government’s judicial overhaul plan began in January, Golov attended one a demonstration and soon became one of thousands of veterans, and now military reservists, who have taken up the cause as their new mission.

Some, including elite Air Force reservists, have taken it a step further, threatening not to heed the call to train or even serve in protest of the government’s plans planned judicial changes, which would give the governing parties more control over Israel’s judiciary.

Others have taken to becoming some of the most active organizers and demonstrators. Last week, a group from Brothers and Sisters in Arms protested by carrying a figure wrapped in the Israeli flag on a stretcher, the way they would carry a wounded comrade off the field.

While Golov says he has not taken the drastic step to refuse service, he understands the motivation.

“We’re fighting for justice and liberty, just like the American story, that’s the values that that are being represented symbolized back when we look at our flag, that’s something that was lacking lacking for the last few decades. So basically, we reclaim the flag,” he said.

Palestinian taxi driver recounts surviving attack by right-wing protesters

Fellow members of the group, all wearing brown shirts with the organization’s logo, come up and say hello. They’re sprinkled all throughout the protests. One is even leading the “Pink Front,” a group of coordinated drummers who look like they are dressed for a rave, and often lead the chants at the protests.

They’re using skills they learned in the military – how to organize, how to mobilize – now for the protests. But more importantly, they say they have the same type of motivation.

“The very deep feeling that you are part of something bigger than yourself, that (you’re) allowed to sacrifice anything that is needed, whether it’s your career, health, seriously mental health,” Golov said. “We all have a mission, you’re willing to do it at any cost. You’re very determined, you know that you are on the right side, you’re carrying the torch of light. That keeps us being highly motivated despite the fact that we’re not sleeping for days.”

Israel’s protest movement is made up of many disparate groups, but the pressure from Israel’s much vaunted veterans has been seen as a key to moving the needle.

Last Monday, after weeks of sustained protests and the largest general strike in Israeli history, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a pause to the legislation, to allow time for negotiations with the opposition.

But despite the announcements, protesters are still out in the streets in large numbers. CNN affiliate Channel 12 in Israel estimated the size of Saturday’s demonstration in Tel Aviv at about 150,000 people. Organizers claimed it was 230,000.

Last week’s mass protests and widespread strike action came after Netanyahu said he had decided to fire Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for advocating a delay in passing the legislation – a move that Netanyahu has since delayed, sources told CNN, due to “the present security situation.”

In his televised speech calling for a delay, Gallant had said the pause in the legislation was needed “for the security of Israel,” citing the refusal of some Israel Defense Forces reservists to train in protest of the government plans. He said pressing ahead with the proposals could threaten Israel’s security.

Under pressure at home and from allies abroad, Netanyahu said he would delay votes on the remaining legislation until after the Knesset’s Passover recess in April “to give time for a real chance for a real debate.”

“Out of the responsibility to the nation, I decided to delay … the vote, in order to give time for discussion,” he added.

But Netanyahu indicated that the delay was only temporary. He insisted that the overhaul was necessary, and reiterated criticism of refusal to train or serve in the military in protest at the planned changes. “Refusing is the end of our country,” he said.

Many protesters don’t believe that the pause is real, or say it’s simply a stalling tactic to give Netanyahu some breathing room and get the protesters to go home before he plows on with the reforms.

“We will start doing deactivation only when we will know 100% that Israel state will stay a functional democratic country. Whatever needs to be done for that,” Golov said.

#153. HIV infections could rise amid aid cuts, UN warns

The impact of United States government funding cuts has been dramatic for many HIV programs, UNAIDS warned. The agency expects that 2027 data to show an increase in new infections after being on the cusp of ending AIDS.

New HIV infections could rise next year for the first time in years, reversing a historic decline amid funding cuts and anti-rights campaigns, the United Nations (UN) warned on Tuesday.

"The world has moved closer towards controlling the HIV pandemic, but changes in funding and resulting service disruptions jeopardize this progress," the UNAIDS agency said in its annual global update.

AIDS-related death numbers has fallen to its lowest in more than two decades. According to the organization, this was made possible by broader access to treatment and improvements in the quality of care programs.

The virus claimed roughly 570,000 lives globally in 2025. This means almost 1,600 people died everyday. In comparison, this figure was 600,000 in 2024 and 1.3 million in 2010.

Based on data from 172 countries, the agency estimated that 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV in 2025, of whom 32.1 million were receiving antiretroviral treatment.

The wider use of antiretroviral medication also reduces the risk of HIV transmission, the organization said. It estimates that 1.2 million people contracted HIV in 2025, down from 1.3 million the year before. The peak in 1994 saw 3.5 million.

"HIV, which was once a death sentence, has become a manageable health condition for millions of people thanks to life-saving HIV medicines," said UNAIDS.

Despite the encouraging data so far, cuts to international funding have hampered efforts to fight HIV, the agency warned.

HIV programs faced an 18-percent decrease in international financing over the past year, said UNAIDS.

"Funding losses have destabilized HIV programs worldwide, coinciding with a wider contraction in official development assistance over the years," it said.

Although the United States remains the largest international donor for HIV programs, its contributions dropped by 26% between 2024 and 2025.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

After dismantling USAID, the world's largest foreign aid agency, last year, the Donald Trump administration has sought to replace decades of aid with new bilateral deals.

"The impact of the United States government funding cuts has been especially dramatic given the reliance of many countries on its support for core HIV programs," said UNAIDS.

Meanwhile disbursements from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria dropped by 13% in 2025.

"We are on the cusp of ending AIDS – this has been the greatest story of global ​health – and just when we should finish it, cuts and the rolling back of human rights is ​threatening to take away our gains," Winnie Byanyima, executive director of UNAIDS, told ​Reuters.

"We haven't ‌got the data yet, but we see the signs. We see all the signs of reversals," she added.

Byanyima predicted that data released in 2027 would begin to reflect a rise in new HIV infections.

In 2015, the UN set a goal to end AIDS by 2030.

#152. Why a Crusoe investor is betting on solar and batteries to power future AI data centers

The problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era. In just a few years, the U.S. grid has gone from basically zero growth to adding several gigawatts a year.

“Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Partners (G2VP), told TechCrunch. “It’s atoms, not bits, and the world is in the process of recognizing the realities of those challenges.”

It’s been a bumpy road. Because it takes a while to scale supply chains, companies have been securing power in any form they can. In many cases, that has meant buying, renting, and deploying natural gas power plants, but Porter thinks that hyperscalers and data center developers should look at the bigger picture if they want to move faster.

That picture involves solar paired with energy storage, based on an analysis Porter and his colleagues at G2VP recently conducted on the state of the data center power market.

“Global capacity of natural gas is only about 60 or 70 gigawatts per year, where solar is already at well over a terawatt,” he said. “Probably the most important lesson that we’ve learned over the last 20 years of backing companies is that Wright’s Law is the thing you want to leverage — making the same thing over and over again.”

Both solar and most forms of long-duration energy storage are built on small, modular technologies that can be manufactured at massive scale. “This is about speed and scale and economics, and we can win across all those dimensions,” Porter said.

G2VP had an early window into AI data center development, having led Crusoe’s Series C. “We’ve had a front-row seat at what’s been happening at that company, how they’ve evolved, how the different waves of data centers have evolved,” Porter said.

The venture firm estimates that data center investment will top $4 trillion until the end of the decade. As the next wave takes shape, the firm sees two different paths for data centers: small, on-grid facilities with their own generating capacity, and larger data centers powered by solar and long-duration energy storage.

“The big idea is to go off-grid,” Porter said. “What that would enable you to do is build with renewables in a way that’s independent of the grid. You can determine your own fate, go around some of the constraints of permitting, whether that’s access to the grid or air permits. You can accelerate your time to market dramatically.”

In recent years, energy storage has been synonymous with lithium-ion batteries, which are too expensive to compete with fossil fuels for round-the-clock power. But a new generation of long-duration energy storage products from the likes of Form Energy and G2VP portfolio company Antora Energy have brought the cost per megawatt-hour down significantly.

Even though the technologies might be a few years away from broad acceptance among data center developers, Porter said they should start thinking about them now.

“It’s analogous to surfing the biggest waves off of Mavericks here in Northern California. The wave is so big that you really have to be paddling and moving and be incredibly nimble to catch it. If you’re at a standstill, it’s just gonna blow you by,” he said.

#148. Uber and Nuro begin driverless testing of Lucid robotaxis ahead of 2027 launch

Uber and Nuro have started testing driverless Lucid Gravity SUVs on public streets in the San Francisco Bay Area more than six months after receiving the permit that allowed the companies to pull the human safety driver from behind the wheel.

The companies will soon begin offering driverless rides to employees in the final lead-up to launching a commercial robotaxi service in the first quarter of 2027.

The milestone comes just 16 months after Uber announced an ambitious plan to launch a premium robotaxi service using Lucid electric vehicles outfitted with autonomous vehicle technology developed by startup Nuro.

That plan came with hefty investments in both companies and much-needed endorsements of their respective products. Uber initially agreed to invest $300 million in Lucid — a figure that has since ballooned to $500 million. Uber also agreed to invest nearly $500 million in Nuro, TechCrunch previously reported, citing sources familiar with the deal.

The agreement provided both Lucid and Nuro with boosts beyond the obvious capital injection. Uber agreed to buy at least 20,000 of Lucid Gravity SUVs over the next six years (a figure that later popped to at least 35,000 vehicles), giving the struggling EV maker a more predictable source of revenue. Nuro, meanwhile, was less than a year removed from announcing a risky, but necessary pivot away from developing driverless delivery vehicles and toward licensing its autonomous vehicle technology to automakers and mobility companies.

Nuro has spent nearly a year testing the Lucid Gravity robotaxi on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area with a human safety operator behind the wheel. The California Department of Motor Vehicles, the agency that regulates the testing and deployment of autonomous vehicles in the state, granted Nuro a driverless AV permit in May 2026.

Uber and Nuro are also testing autonomous vehicles on public roads in Houston with human safety operators behind the wheel. Nuro is supplementing that on-road testing with closed-course testing and simulation to validate the self-driving system before opening the robotaxis to the public. The companies’ combined engineering fleet of autonomous vehicles, which stood at 100 AVs earlier this year, is expanding as Lucid begins manufacturing the first production versions of the robotaxis at its Arizona factory.

The Lucid Gravity robotaxi, unveiled in January 2026, is outfitted with high-resolution cameras, solid-state lidar sensors, and radars that help the self-driving system perceive the real-world environment and operate in it. Uber, which will own and operate the fleet, has focused its efforts on the in-cabin experience, including how riders will interact with the vehicle.
