Given everything moms do for us, it feels good to give back during the holidays. But where to start? How do you come up with a physical representation of how you feel about such a key and influential figure in your life? The possibilities seem as endless as they are daunting, but fear not, we’ve done the hard work for you.

To help you make the mother figure in your life feel truly appreciated, we’ve created a sprawling list of intriguing, lovingly curated gift ideas. From a ring watch and luxe portable gaming deck to a better robovac and an AI-powered bird feeder that brings nature to her doorstep, our list has something to fit all of your mom’s many facets, at a wide range of price points. So take one more thing off your checklist and get her something she’ll truly adore this year.

CDs are back, and it’s not just about the fantastic sound quality. Like vinyl, part of the appeal is the tactile nature of an album on disc. km5’s Cp1 accentuates the vibe with a minimalist form factor that lets you place the jacket art above the disc, plus modern extras like a rechargeable battery and Bluetooth.

Built for jet setters, Anker’s 100W travel adapter features a durable design, a handy LCD display to track charge percentage, and compatibility in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does have four USB inputs for all your portables, including a trio of USB-C ports.

If you’re contemplating a pricey pair of sleep buds for your loved one, we urge you to halt and consider a softer (and cheaper) alternative. Piercing pillows, designed with pockets for freshly pierced ears, also work great for regular earbuds. Blissbury’s comfy and adjustable Ear Pillow is our favorite. Problem — and sleep issues — solved.

SwitchBot’s futuristic block, which is designed to activate physical switches from afar, is as useful as it is eccentric. Also available in a rechargeable configuration, the app-controllable button pusher clips onto almost anything with a switch and lasts up to 600 days on a single 3V CR2 battery.

The BYOK (Bring Your Own Keyboard) is a distraction-free way for creatives to get their thoughts down without the allure of silly YouTube videos or notifications about their dog’s flea meds. No frills, just a low-resolution LCD screen that works with most keyboards and provides plenty of power for the long haul.

If you want to gift your mom something completely different, Bandai’s silly Cup Noodle model offers accurate 3D-scanned details, right down to the egg, shrimp, and “mystery meat.” It’s sure to surprise and delight any hobbyist, especially those with a sense of whimsy.

For the coffee- or tea-loving mom in your life who’s always headed to the microwave for a heat zap, Ember’s fancy-schmancy smart mug is a luxurious way to keep things toasty. With the ability to set the temperature on the mug or in the app, the Mug 3 makes it simple to keep liquids perfectly hot indefinitely.

Govee’s latest lamppost is a nifty gift for any mom looking to light up the yard without invasive procedures. The water-resistant lamp offers 360-degree lighting with adjustable colors at up to 2,000 lumens, built-in motion sensors, a long power cord, and Matter compatibility for versatile smart control.

For any mom after a travel-friendly hair dryer, the Laifen Mini is a must. Affordable, attractive, and powerful, it puts out up to 110,000RPM of drying power in a packable design that weighs well under a pound.

For the mother, father, or other dedicated organizer in your life, enter the P-Touch Cube. The modern label maker offers simple operation and compatibility with iOS and Android, letting users design and personalize custom labels and ribbons on their phones for a fun way to put a label on it.

Soundcore makes some of the best wireless earbuds you’ve never heard of — and the Liberty 5 Pro may be its best pair yet. The sleek buds deliver powerful noise cancellation, good sound, and surprisingly fabulous call quality for way less than Apple’s latest AirPods Pro.

Aura’s aptly titled feeder places its camera beside the feeder instead of inside it, giving you a wider view of nature’s modern dinos. With 2.5K resolution, built-in solar panels, and AI bird identification (all without a pricey subscription), it’s the modern way to bird.

For on-the-go creators, it’s all about capturing the moment in the highest video quality possible. Insta360’s Luna Pro steadycam offers plenty of features to get the job done right, including 4K vertical video, swift file transfers, four hours of battery life, and a detachable touchscreen that doubles as a remote.

If a Kindle won’t quite fit into your favorite traveler’s tight pack job, consider the Xteink X4 Pro. The tiny e-reader is easy to pop into your bag or pocket thanks to its 4.3-inch display, and the latest model offers a backlit touchscreen for a more intuitive way to explore the literary world.

Hoto’s soldering iron is super cool — and by that we mean hot, as it’s able to reach nearly 400 degrees Fahrenheit in about three seconds. The cordless, adjustable iron makes the perfect gift for your favorite DIYer, especially since it features customizable presets for virtually any job.

The future is now, so of course we’ve got screens in sunglasses. The Viture Pro 2 are a slick pair of augmented-reality shades with speakers, micro-OLED screens, and a bonus feature: diopter-adjusting dials, which can sharpen the focus of whatever they’re mirroring from a phone or other device over a USB-C tether. Fancy!

We love JisuLife’s basic but effective cooling fan, which offers simple operation, five speeds, and an LCD battery display. Sure, you could spend a hundred bucks or more on a personal cooler, but the rechargeable 10 S is a stellar — and relatively compact — way to beat the heat on a budget.

We’re not used to talking about “budget” Apple products, but the multicolored MacBook Neo isn’t your average Apple device. The stripped-down MacBook packs enough firepower for everyday tasks, along with a pleasing screen and a terrific mechanical trackpad, giving Mom everything she needs at a manageable price.

It’s time for a smarter robovac. Thankfully, there’s the Matic, which looks less like the rambling discs that pervade the space and more like an actual robot that, well, vacuums. It doesn’t get under beds, but it also doesn’t get stuck under them, and it does a great job providing truly no-fuss cleaning thanks to its superb mapping.

If you haven’t been bombarded by the Hulken yet, it’s a rolling tote that’s blown up online. Designed to hold everything from laundry to an impromptu picnic, the durable bag is beloved for its seemingly bottomless capacity and colorful style, making it a thoughtful gift for fashionable moms on the move.

There’s no shortage of mobile gaming controllers, but few are as stealthy or as compact as the MCON. The sliding gamepad quickly attaches to any MagSafe- or Pixelsnap-ready phone, letting you game with a set of satisfying controls that feel more natural than most rivals.

So what if you’ve heard “Golden” more times than you can count? Netflix’s massive animated hit is a lot easier to gift now that it’s officially available on 4K Blu-ray disc. The story about three pop stars who band together to save humanity from a demonic boy band is an instant classic, with fantastic music and striking animation.

The HoverAir X1 is the hands-off drone your mom didn’t know she needed. Marketed as a “selfie drone,” the autonomous X1 is super light, fits in a small bag, and includes five predetermined flight paths for snapping photos based on your location, with a sixth pattern you can customize.

Digital photos changed everything, but there’s still something wonderful about the visceral touch and nostalgia of analog. Fujifilm’s Instax Mini Evo provides an intriguing hybrid that bridges these worlds, with a retro design, intuitive dials and controls, and the ability to filter like it’s 1989 (or 1889?).

The Varmblixt hits the sweet spot between style and usability. Its donut shape is a vibe, one you can adjust with the included Bluetooth remote to showcase a vibrant palette of colors. A separate hub, meanwhile, adds Ikea, Google, or Apple smart home support, making for a chic yet versatile way to illuminate any living space.

You can help your mom celebrate Miffy’s 70th birthday with Casetify’s artsy iPhone cases, each of which is adorned with stamps, postcards, playful stickers, and — more importantly — the famous Dutch bunny’s adorable figure and iconic blue dress.

Give the gift of prolonged hearing (and brain health) with these fashionable yet functional earplugs from Loop. No one should go anywhere without accessible hearing protection, let alone concerts or other loud events, and Loop’s covert plugs stand out with a commendable 12dB of noise reduction.

Mom works hard, and she deserves some self-care. Even if you can’t send her to a spa, you can bring a bit of luxury home with CeraVe’s fragrance-free eye cream, which is designed to reduce dark circles and remove unwanted puffiness.

Dock & Bay’s blankets are well suited for the new parents in your circle. They provide a soft space on which to entertain young kids, whether at the park or on your hardwood floors at home, and they’re incredibly easy to pack. Plus, they have a water-resistant bottom and come in an array of fun colors.

Experienced moms know blowing up balloons manually is for the birds. Balloon Buddy’s plug-in air inflator makes filling birthday balloons a cakewalk (sorry, not sorry), helping busy parents maximize efficiency so they can move on to other tasks.

If you’re after a luxe PC handheld to satisfy Mom’s gaming habits, the Ally X20 is a sweet machine that supports Xbox, Steam, Epic, and more. Highlights include a luscious 7.4-inch OLED screen, a rotatable trick D-pad, and plenty of power, all housed within a refined translucent body.

If Mom loves nothing more than the clickety-clack of keys as she types her latest email or novella, Wobkey’s Crush 80 Reboot Pro is a radical gift. The packable, tenkeyless board feels straight out of an ’80s computer lab, with satisfying feedback, 10 color options, and extras like RGB lighting.

You probably never thought ring watches would be a thing, let alone a cool thing, but here we are. The G-Shock Nano 5600-1 is based on Casio’s beloved DW5600 from ’87, and if it’s not the cutest and most durable little sports watch in the world, we’re not sure what is.

The new Fitbit Air provides the same great fitness tracking we’ve come to expect in a comfortable design that virtually disappears on your wrist. Google’s AI Coach can be overly assertive, but the tracker’s great battery life and metrics for everything from sleep to blood oxygen make it an excellent gift for anyone who needs a healthy hand.

Nothing can replace our furry friends, so for pets that tend to wander, only the best tracking tech will do. Enter the Fi Ultra, which uses Starlink technology via T-Mobile to track pets almost anywhere, even in cellular dead zones.

#145. A new approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine shows early promise

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

China and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

The US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

As long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, says study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

The immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler said.

Mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with new variants.

The new nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

The researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

“You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler said.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

As promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans

“They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, said Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the new research.

The study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an update.

It also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler says they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss company called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

Other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland said. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a new vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

In reality, Poland said, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

“That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he said.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax says it may not survive

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a company called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team says it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very important in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler said.

They have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

FluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Sign up here to get The Results Are In with Dr. Sanjay Gupta every Tuesday from the CNN Health team.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

Another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler said, so it would have to be used carefully.

#143. Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming

Music streaming service Tidal said on Tuesday that it will start banning and removing songs generated fully with AI in a bid to stem the flood of submissions to its platform. The company said that over the past 90 days, more than 43% of tracks uploaded to its platform were generated by AI, and that was a major reason driving this decision.

Tidal said it will start removing fully AI-generated music on December 9, and the process will result in more than 29 million songs being deleted from the platform by the end of the year. With the new rules in place, the platform said it will be rejecting roughly 80,000-85,000 tracks per day.

Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering 100% AI-generated tracks, and will reject submissions if songs’ metadata says they are made fully using AI.

The company said it will still accept songs that were made with AI assistance, but not fully generated.

The move comes as AI-generated music inundates streaming services across the board. Tidal is one of the first major platforms after Bandcamp to ban AI music outright. Deezer, which also provides detection tools to other streaming services, said that it will introduce a toggle to let users filter out AI music. Larger platforms like Spotify and YouTube Music have adopted a milder approach to this issue, choosing to label AI-generated music instead of offering filters or taking stronger measures.

Tidal started de-monetizing songs made using AI in June, but that did not prove enough of a deterrent, Tidal Music’s lead, Robert Anderson, said on X.

A few months ago, @Tidal tagged and demonetized all wholly AI-generated tracks to protect the authenticity of real artists. But that’s enough, as 43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done…

The company said that 27 million, or 6.3% of tracks on the platform, are fully AI-generated, but 96% of those have no streams.

Meanwhile, music labels are trying to make money by partnering with platforms and AI model makers to sell their catalog for training or remixing features. Goldman Sachs estimates that by 2035, AI-related licensing tools and new monetization opportunities have the potential to improve record labels’ revenue by 10%.

Game modding communities are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC, but one big effort has been taken down by Take-Two today. Leonida, a fan project by 15-year-old “NotRexed,” has vanished after a DMCA takedown notice from GTA VI publisher Take-Two.

Leonida was designed to translate a leaked GTA VI Xbox build to run natively on Windows. Cyberleek, the leaker who posted multiple GTA VI gameplay videos over the summer, published a full Xbox build of the game earlier this week. The leak has kicked recompilation efforts up a notch, as modders race to reverse-engineer the game’s code and rebuild it into native PC code.

Some have managed to get the game to boot on PC, but recompiling the full game won’t be easy — even with help from AI tools like Claude. Take-Two is trying to slow this progress, and its IP enforcement team targeted the main GitHub repository for Leonida and more than 2,900 forks of it, claiming that it “infringes upon Take-Two’s copyrighted works and facilitates copyright infringement of Rockstar Games title, Grand Theft Auto VI.”

PortWatch VI is tracking the efforts to recompile, emulate, or port the leaked Xbox build over to PC. At the time of publishing, the VIctory project and forks of it are leading the way. People are also trying to use XCL, a compatibility layer that runs Xbox Series X games on a Windows PC, to get GTA VI running.

At this point, it seems like Take-Two might not be able to avoid the inevitable here. The clock started ticking down to the release of the PC version last week, and if recent reports are true, we might see it in a few months. If GTA VI is close to being officially ready for PC, we could hear about a release before modders manage to get the game running on PC unofficially.

#141. The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.

'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, new report shows. Here are the key takeaways

Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an important purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.

This shift in consumer preferences has propelled many beauty brands to set environmental goals: to move away from single-use and virgin plastics, provide recyclable, reusable and refillable packaging and offer more transparency around products’ ingredients so customers can ascertain how “green” their purchase is.

However, consumers still struggle to understand the sustainability credentials of many products, according to the British Beauty Council. This is because the industry’s clean-up efforts have been inconsistent, and fall short of making a recognizable impact in the absence of collective goal-setting, global strategy and standardized regulations.

There is no international standard for the beauty industry on how much product ingredient information to share with customers — or how to do so. Brands can set their own rules and goals, giving rise to confusion and “greenwashing,” where sustainability claims are often touted but not substantiated.

Companies often use marketing language like “clean beauty” to make it seem like their products are natural, for example, when they may not actually be organic, sustainable or ethically made.

After rebranding in the West, many beauty companies are still offering to 'whiten' skin elsewhere

“The term ‘clean beauty’ has become quite dangerous. It’s used to sell more products,” according to British Beauty Council CEO Millie Kendall, who added that such buzzwords are losing traction in the UK as British customers wise up to their shortcomings. “Customers need better marketing information and certification information.”

In a 2021 report calling on the industry to have “the courage to change” their business practices, the British Beauty Council wrote that, all too often, even natural ingredients involved in manufacturing products give way to “over-consumption, non-regenerative farming practices, pollution, waste and neglect.”

“The only way out of this is transparency,” Kendall told CNN.

Jen Lee, chief impact officer at US-based brand Beautycounter, said she continues to see confusion over ingredients among consumers. (In 2013, the company launched and published “The Never List,” which currently cites more than 2,800 chemicals — including heavy metals, parabens and formaldehyde — it claims to never use in its products.)

“Natural vs. synthetic ingredients has been a conversation. People think natural is safer, but it’s not always the case,” Lee explained. “Natural ingredients formulated in the industry can have toxic load. Heavy metals can occur in natural components of the earth.”

Mother loses peripheral vision from apparent exposure to mercury in beauty creams. Toxic levels in her home put family at risk, say experts

“We used to be more natural and organic,” added Sasha Plavsic, founder of makeup brand ILIA Beauty. “What was challenging is (that) raw materials were difficult to source or would come in inconsistently or products wouldn’t perform.”

Most makeup is created and molded at high temperatures, Plavsic explained. Purely organic materials often fall apart in this heat, leading to inconsistent results and subpar product performance. “Not every synthetic is bad,” Plavsic said. “Sometimes, it helps create the best in class formula.”

The industry’s plastic packaging is a particular sustainability challenge — 95% is thrown away and the vast majority is not recycled, according to the British Beauty Council.

The cosmetics business is the fourth biggest plastic packaging user globally — after food and beverage, industrial packaging and pharmaceuticals — and plastic is about 67% of the industry’s packaging volume, according to Vantage Market Research. Beauty giant L’Oreal used 144,430 metric tons of plastic in its packaging material in 2021, for example, according to the Ellen Macarthur Foundation (EMF). Estee Lauder Companies reported its brands produced 71,600 metric tons of plastic in product packaging that same year.

And only 9% of the global plastic waste is recycled, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The United States only recycles 4% of its plastic waste.

Single-use plastic is wreaking havoc on the planet. Here's what you can do to minimize your impact

Many brands are trying to phase out harmful plastics from their operations and adopt post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastic. (L’Oreal has set a target of 50% PCR plastic usage by 2025, while Estee Lauder is targeting 25% “or more” PCR plastic — but both are far from achieving their targets.)

“Between 60-70 major global brands have made unprecedented progress” in PCR plastic usage across industries, EMF’s Plastic Initiative Lead Sander DeFruyt told CNN. But DeFruyt stressed that PCR plastic must be adopted in conjunction with brands removing single and virgin plastics from their usage cycles to truly make a difference.

However, PCR plastic is not easy to find — low recycling rates around the world mean there is limited supply. Meanwhile, demand for it is growing demand across industries, DeFruyt said. This competition hikes up its price, which is already higher than virgin plastic.

Hair care brand FEKKAI claims that it used up to 95% PCR content in its packaging, but pricing and supply issues posed a challenge, forcing it to currently aim for containers and packaging that feature at least 50% PCR in its packaging.

“PCR plastic is more expensive than stock plastic. The cost is hard and then sourcing it is too,” founder Frédéric Fekkai told CNN. “PCR is close to our heart, but there is a massive demand, so finding recycled plastic is difficult.”

Beauty retailers plays a pivotal — and under-utilized — role, with control over stocking decisions and supply chains. But many vary when it comes to the standards they set for brands they sell.

“Smaller businesses do more, full stop,” said Jessi Baker, founder of the technology platform Provenance, which helps brands display their sustainability credentials for customers. “They move more nimbly. Some of them are born-good brands — climate friendliness was part of their setup. They don’t need to restructure their entire supply chain. Their culture already has it compared to the larger brands who need to work hard to change.”

A history of beauty trends -- and the standards that shaped them

Sephora launched its “Clean + Planet Positive” initiative in 2021, which labeled products that met its set criteria. (This is separate from the French retailer’s “Clean at Sephora” program, which is currently facing a consumer lawsuit alleging it carries a significant percentage of products understood by customers to be harmful.) Target launched a similar program in 2022, featuring a “Target Zero” icon for both online and in-store offerings that either have reusable, recyclable, compostable or reduced plastic packaging, or feature waterless or concentrated products.

Still, many steps taken by brands and retailers do not even begin to touch on the waste and pollution generated throughout supply chains, manufacturing and shipping, all huge problems for the industry to grapple with.

The gaps in standardization in the beauty ecosystem can, to some extent, be filled by certifications such as the US-born B Corporation, or B Corp. This accreditation, one of the most well-known in the beauty space, is issued by the non-profit B Lab, which scores a company on a variety of criteria around ethics and sustainability. However beneficial it may be among eco-conscious consumers, though, it is currently completely voluntary for brands to apply for.

Governments and multinationals enforcing regulations and setting a base line for brands to operate from when making sustainability claims would go a long way to making change, many experts and business leaders believe.

Susanne Kaufmann, founder of her namesake beauty brand, says her efforts in Austria would reap better results if more countries around the world had stricter, more uniform garbage disposal laws.

A trash heap 62 meters high shows the scale of India's climate challenge

“I package our product in a recyclable material,” Kaufmann said. (Her products’ packaging, which is refillable and reusable, is made from 75% recycled plastic — and is 100% recyclable.) If I send this to the US, the garbage is not separated… and it’s not recyclable,” she explained, referring to inconsistencies in recycling laws across the United States.

And when it comes to ingredients, the European Chemicals Agency lists 2,495 substances banned from use in cosmetic products marketed for sale or use in the bloc. But the US Food and Drug administration only lists 11, making it more challenging for American consumers to find safer, greener options. The Environmental Working Group, a non-profit watchdog, studied lab tests of 51 sunscreen products in 2021 and found that only 35% of products met the EU standard, compared with 94% that passed the US standard.

However, while government can set minimum requirements, Mia Davis, vice president of sustainability and impact at beauty retailer Credo Beauty, says the needle will move in the private sector.

Sustainable ships: The world's most eco-conscious cruises

“Regulation can raise the floor a bit. A person who doesn’t know about any (sustainability issues) should still be able to walk into a bodega and get clean products… But that’s never going to be what the market can do,” she said. “Market leadership is key.”

In the absence of bold regulations or global standards on sustainability practices, this “leadership” — undertaken both by brands and customers in the beauty marketplace — is likely to be the most immediately impactful vector for addressing the industry’s climate shortcomings. It will take continued collective advocacy and initiative to see meaningful climate-conscious change.

#140. Meta brings its Muse AI assistant directly into Instagram DMs

Instagram users can now chat with Meta’s AI agent Muse in a DM thread, the company announced on Tuesday. The social media network says users can chat with Muse to get more context about a post, place, or product they come across, or catch up on conversations they may have missed in their other DMs.

The new integration gets rid of the need for users to toggle between Instagram and the Muse app when they want to interact with the AI agent. It also reflects the growing competition among tech companies to make AI assistants a part of users’ everyday digital lives. By embedding Muse directly into Instagram, Meta is making it easier for users to access the AI agent, while also giving Muse access to a platform where users already discover products, places, and content.

Users can share Instagram posts with Muse and ask it to take action, such as adding a coffee shop to their Mexico City itinerary or finding a Black Friday deal on a pair of shoes.

Meta notes that conversations with Muse on Instagram will appear as a side chat in the main Muse app.

Muse in Instagram DMs will begin rolling out on Tuesday for iOS and Android users in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Japan, and Singapore.

Meta also announced that users can now do more with the posts and reels they’ve bookmarked on Instagram. For example, they can ask Muse to organize their saved content into custom folders, known as Collections. They could also ask Muse to turn a recipe video into a grocery list, turn the travel content from their favorite travel creators into an itinerary for an upcoming trip, or have Muse send them outfit ideas based on fashion reels they’ve collected.

Starting Tuesday, when users save a post on Instagram, they will see a prompt for Muse to organize it for them. This feature is launching in the U.S. and Canada.

Meta says that users remain in control of their Muse experience on Instagram. Nothing is shared, published, or sent without their approval, and they can ask Muse to forget information or undo actions at any time.

#139. Ukraine's bid for NATO membership and more air defense remains controversial

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is calling for the rapid acceptance of his country into NATO. However, the necessary unanimity for this is lacking, as shown during the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.

It took a while for the video call to connect. When Volodymyr Zelenskyy finally greeted the delegates in Berlin, applause broke out. The Ukrainian president appealed to the gathered parliamentarians from 32 NATO member states to keep supporting his country, especially against the massive aerial bombardment from Russia.

"Dear friends, winter is now ahead of us. And of course, our number one priority is air defense," Zelenskyy told the delegates. His country urgently needs more Patriot and other comprehensive anti-air attack systems. "And your countries have them. Missiles that can stop Russian ballistic missiles should not be sitting in warehouses collecting dust. And we say this openly. Please help us with this."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Zelenskyy renewed his call for his country to join the NATO military alliance. That issue is not for the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, which was gathered for its 72nd annual meeting in Berlin, to decide. But it was important to the Ukrainian president to reiterate his request.

After the war ends, Ukraine needs strong security guarantees and NATO could ensure those. "Wouldn't it be more effective to simply bring Ukraine into NATO?" Zelenskyy asked, arguing: "Wouldn't that be better for all of us, for everyone? Cheaper to put in place? And more reliable when it comes to actually protecting security?"

There is conflict among NATO members about the possibility of admitting Ukraine. The alliance has affirmed multiple times that the path to membership stands open to Ukraine — however, in the long term rather than the near future. This is primarily because of the ongoing war and the possible assistance obligations of other NATO countries for Ukraine, which was attacked by Russia.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte rejected the Ukrainian demands at the summit, which for the first time in 26 years was held in Berlin. Ukraine had entry prospects; however, NATO members currently lack unanimity on this issue. NATO alone decides who becomes a member. "There is total clarity on that within the alliance," Rutte said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz advocated for Ukraine to receive security guarantees similar to what NATO members have, in the instance of a possible ceasefire. In retrospect, it was clear "what a mistake it was not to follow the American suggestion back in 2008 at the NATO summit in Bucharest to admit Ukraine as a member," Merz said at a joint press conference following a meeting with Rutte.

Whether or not a NATO entry for Ukraine could be part of negotiations with Russia is another question, according to Rutte. He approved of current US efforts to bring about peace talks, and how Europe was closely consulting with Ukraine and the US for a unified position. "But it is also to test now whether Putin is willing to play ball, and then these issues might come up again."

The Russian invasion of Ukraine has led to NATO arming itself on a massive scale. Members have committed to raising their countries' defense spending to 5% of their gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035.

Rutte warned that all the allies needed a credible path to get there, "and ideally, they get there sooner than 2035." In addition, he said weapons production among member states needed to further increase because "right now, demand still far exceeds the supply."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The contribution by Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces to NATO was explained by Carsten Breuer, Germany's highest-ranking soldier. For example, the massive increase in military spending: "Our defense budget has tripled since 2021. The goal is to achieve the 5% target, which was set at the summit in The Hague, well before 2035." In the coming year, Germany's defense budget has risen to more than €139 billion ($151 billion).

The Bundeswehr was further developing into a "constantly modernized, effective and innovative army, Breuer said. Also, a much larger one than before. "To reach our current capability goals we are expanding the Bundeswehr to a total of 460,000 soldiers by the mid-2030s," the German chief of defense said. Of those, 200,000 are to be reservists. "This is like walking a tightrope because we must find the right balance between growth and operational readiness."

Following his speech, Breuer answered questions from the delegates who showed keen interest in the developments. The discussion was a preview of Breuer's new post: He has been voted in as the new chair of the NATO Military Committee and will move to the alliance's headquarters in Brussels mid-next year. Then he will become the principal military advisor to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. "I take this election as a sign of recognition that Germany has now accepted its responsibility as well as its role in security policy," Breuer said.

A jury has found Huawei guilty of stealing US trade secrets, as reported earlier by NBC News and Bloomberg. The verdict, handed down in a federal court in New York, concludes a years-long legal battle that accused the Chinese telecom giant of stealing source code and proprietary technology from several companies, including T-Mobile, Cisco, and Motorola.

The Department of Justice’s 2018 criminal indictment against Huawei came to light following the arrest of the company’s CFO, Wanzhou Meng, whom the agency accused of fraud. Though the indictment against Meng was eventually dismissed, she admitted to misleading banks over Huawei’s operations in Iran as part of a deferred prosecution agreement. The US government blacklisted Huawei in 2019 over national security concerns.

In total, the jury found Huawei guilty of 10 of 12 criminal counts, including money laundering, violating US sanctions, bank fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy to defraud the US. The company was acquitted of engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice. Huawei’s sentencing is set for September 14th, 2027, where it may face “financial penalties including criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution,” according to the DOJ.

“For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft, and deception,” Tysen A. Duva, the assistant attorney general of the DOJ’s criminal division, says in a statement. “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security.”

In a statement to NBC News, a Huawei spokesperson said the charges are “without legal or factual merit” and that it plans to appeal the decision. Huawei didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

#136. Electric truck startup Harbinger gets financing boost from Palmer Luckey’s bank

Harbinger has tapped Palmer Luckey’s Erebor Bank as a new source of capital as the electric truck startup looks to diversify how it funds its growth and an expanding portfolio of products spanning autonomous vehicles, energy storage, and defense.

Los Angeles-based Harbinger said Tuesday it secured more than $100 million in financing, including a convertible note from Pinegrove Venture Partners and senior debt from Erebor Bank, which launched in February 2026 and recently surpassed $1 billion in loans, according to the Financial Times.

The new financing comes less than three weeks after Harbinger raised $240 million in a Series D funding round co-led by Tiger Global, Capricorn’s Technology Impact Fund, and Ridgeline. FedEx, which ordered 2,000 trucks from Harbinger, also participated.

Harbinger co-founder and chief executive John Harris explained in a statement that building an industrial technology company at scale requires a “different financing approach,” adding that the capital needed to ramp up production and deliver vehicles to customers shouldn’t have to come entirely from equity. Harris noted that major vehicle and aerospace manufacturers have long relied on debt financing to support their production operations.

Erebor is now Harbinger’s primary banking partner. In a statement, Luckey said traditional lenders have struggled to support the unique capital needs of businesses developing real technology and creating U.S. jobs.

“Harbinger is exactly the kind of business we built Erebor to back: an American manufacturer building world-class technology,” he said.

#135. Why the US Army is about to blow up nearly 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives in Iowa

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The US Army is scrambling to contain any potential lead pollution that could spread if an old stockpile of explosives blows up.

The US Army is scrambling to contain any potential lead pollution that could spread if an old stockpile of explosives blows up.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The US Army is moving ahead with plans to detonate the nation’s stockpile of lead azide at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, at approximately 9:00AM CST on Wednesday. The Verge reached out to experts on what to expect, and will keep this post updated.

What material is the Army planning to detonate?

There are 68 drums holding about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, an unstable chemical compound created to detonate munitions like grenades. The US started using lead azide as a primary explosive almost a century ago before “moving away” from it about 15 years ago because of how difficult the material is to store and transport, Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), said in a Tuesday press briefing. At that point, the US transferred its remaining stockpile of lead azide to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. Lead azide will explode at 350 degrees Celsius (662F). But it is also sensitive to flame, friction, or sudden shock, including fluctuations in temperature.

Some of the material on site in Iowa is more than 60 years old. The material can crystallize as it degrades over time, becoming unstable enough to explode even at ambient temperatures. The Army noted some deterioration of the material in 2009 — but not any “dangerous crystallization” at the time, according to Cekada.

“It’s not a matter of if, it’s a matter of when.”

The chemical was stored in liquid form, embedded in sawdust and burlap bags inside the drums. Water and ethanol were also added to the containers to keep the lead azide from freezing in the winter. But during a March inspection, Cekada said ATF noticed “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels.” That made the material too unstable for them to open the barrels to add more water and ethanol, Cekada said. Removing a lid might cause the barrels to detonate.

Officials have been trying to figure out what to do with the crystallized lead azide since that alarming March inspection. The Army initially hired a contractor to safely dissolve the chemicals but canceled the contract earlier this year, according to reporting by The New York Times. Using a chemical neutralization agent “proved to be an unsafe method,” Army Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the 71st Explosive Ordinance Disposal Group, said at the Tuesday briefing, because crystallization on the outside of the barrels made it too risky to open the lids.

“Everyone that we’ve spoken to through their experience has determined that this is the only safe path forward,“ Cekada said at the briefing. If they leave the chemicals as is, he said, they’re still at risk of exploding. “It’s not a matter of if, it’s a matter of when.”

Compared to an uncontrolled, spontaneous explosion, a controlled detonation is supposed to limit the amount of lead dust unleashed on surrounding communities and the environment. Still, the dust plume could reach as far as 100 miles away from the site. The Army has released maps showing where lead dust is expected to travel based on its modeling.

The last time the Army disposed of lead azide this way at a comparable scale was in 1977, according to Teller. At the time, they detonated 7,000 pounds of the material in Colorado in open air “with zero mitigation.” Even then, 75 percent of the lead particulate stayed on site, Teller said at the briefing. The Army now believes it can “significantly reduce” the spread of that last 25 percent of lead using walls made up of four 16,000-gallon water tanks to capture lead particulate and hopefully prevent it from escaping into the atmosphere.

The 80-year-old earth-covered magazines holding the lead azide are cracked and deteriorating, Teller noted, and they are likely to break open after the detonation. To prepare, they’ve covered it with tarp and a special containment screen for lead. They also plan to flood it with 2 feet of foam to capture particulate pollution. Adam Telle, Acting Secretary of the Army, also said the Army has set out “state of the art gel blocks in huge quantities all around to ensure that we absorb as much of this blast as we possibly can.”

There is no “safe” level of exposure to lead

Last week, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club sought a court order to stop the explosion from taking place, pending an Environmental and Health Impact Statement and an investigation into alternatives to detonating the material. President Donald Trump chimed in on social media, calling for a pause until a federal appeals court gave the Army the green light after previously granting a temporary stay. The court on Monday denied the emergency motion to stop the explosion, clearing the way for the Army to move forward.

The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services (Iowa HHS) recommends that anyone in potentially affected areas stay indoors and keep windows shut for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation. Iowa HHS also suggests switching off HVAC systems that might bring outdoor air inside or set them to modes that recirculate air, and using an air purifier with a HEPA filter.

FEMA is helping relocate Middletown residents and others within a voluntary 5-mile evacuation zone. People who are pregnant, children, and individuals with chronic diseases should evacuate the affected areas, Sean Kaufman, principal deputy assistant secretary for preparedness and response at the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, said at the briefing. “Outside of that area, if you’re close to that proximity and you’re uncomfortable, I think you need to do what you need to do to take care of your family,” Kaufman said.

There is no “safe” level of exposure to lead, a neurotoxin that poses health risks when inhaled or ingested. Kids are at increased risk because their brains are still developing and are also more likely to touch contaminated surfaces and then stick their fingers in their mouths. But most adverse health effects — which can include fatigue and gastrointestinal upset alongside impacts on brain development — are connected to chronic lead exposure rather than as a result of a one-off event.

“It is likely this exposure will not result in any observable acute clinical signs,” Will Sander, associate professor of preventive medicine and public health at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, says in an email to The Verge. “Overall, the risk is minimal, and there should be no long-term concerns.”

“The Army has done this before a long time ago and took lead measurements afterward that were low but hazardous (in my opinion),” Chris Kohler, an adjunct instructor at Indiana University who is an expert on hazardous waste, environmental remediation, and chemical hygiene, says in an email to The Verge. “The detonation will spread lead in the atmosphere. Not a desirable outcome.” Kohler and other experts say it’ll be important to continue monitoring the explosion site and surrounding areas to see if there needs to be any more remediation.

#133. Threads comes to iPad and takes a page from X’s playbook with cashtags

It may have taken 15 years for Instagram to launch on the iPad, but Instagram’s other app, Threads, has taken a slightly faster path to the Apple tablet. In an overnight update, the company rolled out a big-screen version of the X competitor. It’s also added another new feature, borrowed from X: the stock-tracking feature known as cashtags.

While the iPad version of the app works well in portrait orientation, some users are disappointed to find that the landscape layout doesn’t work as they’d expect. Instead of offering a multi-column interface as on Threads’ web app, the iPad app focuses on the user’s main feed in a single-column layout. There are also options to swipe right and left from the main screen to access the search screen and the feeds menu, respectively.

The iPad app isn’t the company’s only update in the latest release. According to a post from Threads engineer Guy Dickinson, Threads will now support cashtags — a feature popularized by Twitter years ago for tracking live stock information. These specialized tags start with the dollar sign (“$”) followed by a ticker symbol. When you click on a cashtag, you can follow the discussions around the stock.

In addition, Threads is adding live stock quotes, charts, and other context at the top of each cashtag’s page. As you search for a particular cashtag, the autocomplete search results will display the stock’s current price and the percentage it’s up or down. Dickinson says the feature will currently support NYSE and Nasdaq stocks, ETFs, and crypto. Cashtags will be supported on the web, iOS, and Android. However, they’re just now rolling out, so you may not immediately see them.

The update points to Threads’ broader ambition to compete with X, not only as a destination for discussions about various topics, but also as a place where people can track real-time news and information. Cashtags in particular could attract traders and investors to Threads who typically rely on X.

Despite facing stiff competition from X, Meta announced earlier this year that Threads topped 500 million monthly users, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says the company believes the app is on track to reach a billion users over time.

#132. The Verge’s 2026 gift guide for dads

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

This year, why not get Dad a gift or two he won’t expect?

This year, why not get Dad a gift or two he won’t expect?

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Gone are the days when you could just buy your father a random tie or some leather-clad alcohol vessel or a shaving kit. Dads want — nay, deserve — something memorable. Luckily for you, it’s not that hard to find something special that he’ll approve of, and we’re here to guide you.

We’ve curated this year’s gift list with the modern father in mind, whether he’s a gamer, creator, chef, or simply a gadget lover. There’s a lot in here we think he’ll like, from noise-canceling headphones like the Sonos Ace Ultra and an autonomous drone to a brilliant QD-OLED monitor and a nifty light that’s perfect for illuminating his next campsite. Whatever your dad is into, we’ve got you covered.

Cleaning gadgets like Dyson’s PencilVac FluffyCones are never cheap, but they’re often worth the cost and a pleasure to use. The lightweight, broom-replacing stick vacuum doesn’t do carpets, but its rolling bars pack incredible cleaning power for touching up hard floors, including stairs.

Give the gift that fixes past home improvement transgressions. These handy Japanese-made pliers from Vampire Tools have one fundamental purpose — to remove stripped screws — and they’re damn good at it. The best part? Watching Dad’s face light up seconds before he sprints to the garage for them.

Who would have thought a simple hook could make roaming the city with a backpack so much more convenient? After testing Peak Design’s well-designed bags, we’re convinced the clever addition is a game-changer for anyone who doesn’t want to leave their bag on the filthy ground.

Give your father a little nostalgia and a lot of convenience in one package with this stylish USB-C dock and SSD combo gadget. The cassette-shaped Sharge Disk Pro 2 works as a hub with support for HDMI at 4K, SD and microSD card slots, USB-A and USB-C ports, along with up to 8TB of storage stored within.

It’s time to help Dad ditch his collection of plastic reusable cups, which have clearly seen better days. NotNeutral’s hand-pressed, timeless tumbler offers ’70s vibes with a modern twist, making it the perfect vessel for whatever Dad twists into his favorite drink.

For those who love travel but hate the constraints of a hotel TV, Belkin’s ConnectAir is a slick solution. Plug the transmitter into any device with a USB-C video-out port and the receiver into the TV’s HDMI port, and voilà, you’re easily (and wirelessly) connected.

Have you broken something fragile that seems impossible to mend? Maybe all you need is a Kintsugi Repair Kit, which provides the Japanese method and a special lacquer to repair and restore broken ceramics to good health. The resulting golden scar is merely to remind us that rebuilding is possible.

Werewolf’s affordable dongle kit provides an almost magical way to power nearly any DC device from a USB-C charger or portable battery. Program it from a mobile app, connect it to your old gear, and everything from a PC monitor to an original Game Boy can accept USB-C charging.

If your father already owns an Apple Watch, the Nomad Stratos is a foolproof upgrade idea. The refined watch band features titanium links with a rubbery interior for durable comfort, and it comes in an array of subtle color options that make it as suitable for the office as it is for the slopes.

If you’re after a cheap, useful stocking stuffer, Trond’s reliable three-prong extension cord is a practical pick that’s available in leftward or rightward configurations to fit nearly any outlet. Dad will probably say, “Oh, I’ve always wanted one of these,” and this time he’ll mean it.

The CS-Pro will make your dad feel like a private eye in the early ’80s. The retro-inspired digital camera serves up 16-megapixel stills and offers four filters accessible from its tactile dial, plus USB-C charging, a high-quality Xenon flash, and a 4GB SD card for plenty of vintage photo fun.

Antigravity’s A1 is the ultimate gadget for the dad who dreams of owning the sky. The compact drone comes with specialized goggles that will make him feel like he’s in the cockpit, and it records always-on, 360-degree 8K video. It’s an exhilarating flight experience and an excellent creator’s tool in one slick package.

Sonos raised its headphones game on all fronts with the Ace Ultra, which deliver better noise canceling, improved sound, and the feature we’ve all been waiting for: Wi-Fi support. With the ability to bounce audio across your Sonos ecosystem, including from a TV via newer Sonos soundbars, Dad’s sonic sanctuary is finally complete.

WiiM’s first soundbar builds on its seamless Sonos-esque connectivity with a sleek design, detailed sound, and up-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos spatial audio. It also pairs with other speakers for surround sound through a no-fuss setup process, including ones you already own that are linked to one of WiiM’s amplifiers.

Your dad needs an awesome monitor, but there are 10 billion options. Alienware’s 34-inch Penta Tandem QD-OLED delivers top-end picture quality, with vibrant colors and perfect blacks, plus a swift 280Hz refresh rate. Best of all, it’s not nearly as expensive as you might think.

If your dad is still reading books on his phone (or aging e-reader), it’s time for an upgrade. The latest in Amazon’s series of waterproof, auto-dimming e-readers loads books faster than the prior model and offers a slick aluminum upgrade. No matter which you choose, it’s a better way to bring the library along.

Oura didn’t reinvent the wheel with the Ring 5, but it did reshape it into a slimmer, thinner, more wearable design that could make all the difference. Inside are the same extensive health and fitness tracking features for charting everything from sleep to heart health, backed by long battery life.

Smart TVs are often pretty dumb. If your dad is always complaining about his TV, or if you want to get ahead of it, grab the latest Apple TV 4K. Although it’s not cheap, it stands out with built-in mics for Siri AI, lots of power, HomePod surround sound support, and a simple, ad-free interface.

The Switch 2 leverages the same ideas as its predecessor, only with a larger, 7.9-inch display, a faster chip, and a bevy of new social features. However, its most important trait is that it’s the newest Nintendo console, which means access to a host of weird, beautiful, family-friendly games that only Nintendo could dream up, now on a better screen.

BougeRV’s fancy, compact lamp will spark joy for the glamper in your life, as well as everyone else. Its powerful, foldable spread of LEDs provides a blast of light anywhere plug-ins can’t reach, from the beach to the shed where that scary spider holds court, with up to 60 hours of light on low power.

The Rival Pro offers plenty of thoughtful extras, including swappable batteries and an ultra-wideband base station for a seamless, low-latency connection. The gaming mouse’s lightweight design and 8,000Hz polling rate also deliver both accurate and ergonomic performance for up to 16 hours per charge.

For the manga or live-action Netflix show lover on your list, this fashionable Pirates jersey, inspired by Monkey D. Luffy from the seminal pirate adventure series One Piece, will be as surprising as it is delightful.

Zero Company, a strategy game set in the twilight of the Clone Wars, is a fun way to get lost in the Star Wars universe. The single-player, turn-based title lets players command a diverse team of characters across a gorgeous expanse of worlds, offering hours of solitary entertainment.

We fell for Apple’s handy iPhone strap due to its effortless accessibility and comfy design, which uses flexible magnets to keep excess segments in check. From biking to hiking to concerts, it’s a great way to sling your iPhone 18 Pro, assuming you have a compatible phone case.

The new Fitbit Air provides the same great fitness tracking we’ve come to expect in a comfortable design that virtually disappears on your wrist. Google’s AI Coach can be overly assertive, but the tracker’s great battery life and metrics for everything from sleep to blood oxygen make it an excellent gift for anyone who needs a healthy hand.

Most of us have thousands of photos in the cloud, but if a photo never makes it into the real world, did it really happen? Existentialism aside, the Cricut StickerPix offers a new way to play with photos, providing you with everything you need to turn any picture into a pro-quality print or sticker.

This battery-powered fan is a big upgrade over your average plug-in job. As a 3D circulator, it can tilt to push air in all directions. It can be controlled from an app and even detaches from its stand to sit on a desk or tabletop. Quiet, powerful, and versatile, it’s equipped for nearly any adventure on or off the grid.

If your favorite cinephile is looking to get off the streaming carousel, the Kaleidescape Strato E is the key. The premium player lets library builders locally store and play their favorite films and TV shows in lossless 4K resolution with Dolby Atmos for sterling entertainment that’s all theirs.

Once The Great British Baking Show becomes an obsession, only a serious stand mixer will do for replicating recipes at home. This mixer’s timeless design adds new features in what KitchenAid calls its biggest upgrade since 1955, with a new half-speed setting and a control lever that lets you set speeds between its standard settings.

The Pocket Scion is unlike any musical instrument you’ve witnessed before, one that uses the “biofeedback” from plants to trigger built-in synths. The device offers MIDI-out to send digital signals to outboard synths, and it includes an app for both macOS and Windows, finally giving you a way to make your favorite fern a rockstar.

When it comes to jotting down notes, there’s nothing like a pen and paper. At least, that’s what we thought before we tried the Remarkable Paper Pure. Offering a strikingly realistic writing experience that saves everything in the digital realm, this tablet is a brilliant way to bridge the gap and save paper.

Electronics are becoming more sustainable, and Fairphone is leading the way. The Fairphone 6 Plus may seem like a regular Android phone on paper, but the ability to repair and replace its internals, from the screen to the battery, makes it anything but average.

#131. Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million users a month.

But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.

And once installed, it’s tough to remove.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

Multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Company insiders said the exploits were utilized to spy on users and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” said Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.

“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”

This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.

Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.

Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

The revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational company with roots in China.

While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

There is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any company operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.

The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.

An ensuing report from Bloomberg said a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.

Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”

CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.

Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.

Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).

It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

Pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly users until the end of 2018, the year it listed in New York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the company set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the company only targeted users in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they said.

By collecting expansive data on user activities, the company was able to create a comprehensive portrait of users’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.

This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting users to open the app and place orders, they said.

The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.

PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

Google Play is not available in China, and Android users in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it said it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.

“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” said Hyppönen.

The app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen said. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.

Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.

The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers said.

They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.

“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they said.

In China, about three quarters of smartphone users are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.

Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, said Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.

CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.

Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.

“I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he said.

Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

Toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he said.

Pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he said.

I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive.

According to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to users’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he said.

Of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews showed that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” said René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

Suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread quickly among other researchers, who did name the company. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.

Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a new update of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.

Two days after the update, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

The next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the company’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to big data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source said.

Most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.

A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they said.

Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the update, said although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.

Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Big Tech that began in late 2020.

That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology launched a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.

The Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.

Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

“This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” said Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”

Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.

They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.

CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.

On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

“Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.
